9ccf8665576aaeb3: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world.

These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech).

Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post.

But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress.

On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead.

It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)
The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control.

But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China.

It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further.

What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell.

But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good.

The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

3ec3fbaaa5e4180c: It’s been eight years since NordPass released the first edition of its most common passwords of the year list, and the world has learned nothing about password security in the meantime.
NordPass’ eighth edition of its most common passwords list, as culled from data breaches, was released Monday, and it looks suspiciously like the previous ones in the worst possible way.
“Once again, ‘123456’ is the most commonly used password in the world,” NordPass said in the report. “That makes it seven out of eight years this password has stood at the top of the leaderboard.”

Even when 123456 wasn’t number one, it was still near the top of the heap, as the top three passwords in the list remain unchanged in the eight years NordPass has published its list: 123456, admin, and 12345678. It’s not like the rest of the most common passwords are showing any variety either.

According to NordPass, the only real shuffling among the 10 most popular passwords was the entry of the worryingly short 1234 into the top ten and the migration of the ever-popular password “password” down slightly in the top 10 from 6th to 7th place.
“We still have a lot of work to do to spread awareness about password safety,” NordPass concluded of that data – and there’s no more pressing time than the present.

AI adoption has made password cracking an easier exercise than ever, with more credentials being sucked up in more data breaches at a faster pace. AI has also made cracking hashed passwords a snap too. In other words, if you’re reusing a password that’s been exposed in a breach, even if it’s just a hash that was exposed, you’re more likely than ever before to have another account compromised.
The best advice NordPass gives is to move away from passwords toward biometric authentication or passkeys and you're insane not to enable MFA.
But for the places you still have to use passwords, there are a few things to avoid – like the 200 passwords in NordPass’ list, for example.
Beyond that, NordPass also recommends steering clear of pop cultural trends.

“Fandoms make for terrible passwords,” NordPass notes. There are several reasons for that – namely the fact that they follow trends, meaning that “minecraft” password in the early 2000s was a simple one to add to a password stuffing dictionary, just like “skibiditoilet” in recent years.
The one thing that connects all those pop-culture passwords is that “they all could be cracked in seconds,” NordPass said.

We’re sure our readers are conscientious about their online habits, carefully protecting their accounts with the proper security measures and ensuring each and every password is unique, long, complicated, and random. Unfortunately for you smarties reading El Reg, the person down the hall whose security you’re responsible for may not be so disciplined, so be sure you’re enforcing good practices – Nord knows the average user just isn’t doing it despite years of begging and reminders. ®

ff0169702f8be68d: The researcher who sounded the alarm over Dirty Frag earlier this year has uncovered another Linux kernel flaw, and this one lets attackers crash entire servers remotely without so much as a password.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288 and dubbed NoisyTCP, was discovered by security researcher Hyunwoo Kim, who says it affects almost all Linux distributions. The flaw dates back to October 2015 and went unnoticed until this year, when Kim found and patched it.

Attackers don't need to log in or get their hands on any credentials to cause trouble. They can simply knock the server over, although there's no evidence yet that the flaw can be used to steal data or hijack a machine.

The bug is buried in Linux's TCP networking code. Two parts of the kernel can trip over each other while processing incoming traffic, leaving one trying to use memory that's already been freed. When that happens, Linux can panic and take the whole machine down with it.

Kim says there's no need for any special server configuration either. Services such as Nginx, Apache, and SSH can be vulnerable straight out of the box. An attacker needs access to an open TCP port on a system that processes incoming network traffic across multiple receive queues or CPUs.

Perhaps more concerning for administrators running containerized workloads, the damage isn't necessarily limited to the application being attacked. Because the flaw sits in the Linux kernel, crashing a web server inside a container can take down the underlying host and anything else running on it.

Kim found that the attack was particularly effective against virtual machines. During testing, he managed to crash Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers running on QEMU/KVM virtual machines in between five seconds and two minutes.
Physical hardware put up more of a fight. Even after tailoring his exploit to the target machine, Kim needed roughly 14 hours to crash a bare-metal server running Nginx.

Kim has a knack for finding holes in Linux. Back in May, he uncovered Dirty Frag, a kernel bug that allowed local users to gain root privileges. That one caused headaches for administrators when a working exploit went public before patches were ready.

His latest discovery, NoisyTCP, has another potentially nasty trick up its sleeve. Kim identified a second exploitation path involving a use-after-free condition, although pulling it off is considerably more difficult than simply crashing a server.

In his advisory, Kim says he has developed a limited exploit targeting virtual machines in a lab environment but has yet to demonstrate a general-purpose remote code execution attack. For the moment, the confirmed impact is remote denial of service.

A fix was committed to the upstream Linux kernel on November 3, but administrators will need to check whether their distribution has shipped an updated kernel. Red Hat has rated the vulnerability Important, assigning it a CVSS score of 7.5.
For those unable to patch immediately, Kim suggests two temporary workarounds: disabling TCP SYN cookies or restricting incoming packet processing to a single receive queue.

Neither is particularly appealing. Disabling SYN cookies reduces protection against SYN flood attacks, while limiting packet processing can hurt network performance. The former also needs to be applied separately to containers using their own network namespaces.

Kim published the details on November 15, once the disclosure embargo was lifted. The bug had been hiding in plain sight since 2015, leaving Linux servers vulnerable to remote crashes for 11 years. Not bad for a flaw that doesn't even require a login. ®

2cb18a210c5dea98: Canonical is offering Ubuntu Pro users an opt-in channel for AI-generated security patches, deploying bots to help tackle the growing pile of vulnerabilities other bots are uncovering.

Canonical's VP for "Excellence Engineering," Pierre Guillemin, gave the second keynote at the recent Ubuntu Summit, introducing the Edge archive, an optional repository of security fixes generated by the company's Surge framework.

As the announcement describes it: "We built Surge, a multi-agent orchestration framework for CVE remediation and backporting, and have reached a high level of confidence in its capabilities. We will not automatically upload Surge-generated fixes to our stable releases, but from today they are available to Ubuntu Pro users in the new Edge archive."

Edge offers patches before extended testing and qualification are complete, allowing users to assess them themselves. Canonical says updates delivered through the normal security channels will remain human-validated.
Ubuntu Summit now runs twice a year. Last week's Ubuntu Summit 26.10 followed a rather unfortunately timed server outage for the company.

At the previous such event in June, the company announced a move into agentic AI, but this new one is bolder still. Guillemin noted that "October 2026 saw almost as many CVEs as all of 2025." Surge is a "multi-agent orchestration framework" to remediate vulnerabilities in Ubuntu's userspace. In other words, not the kernel, but even so, it is ambitious.

The idea is to use a group of different LLMs to triage new vulnerabilities, find existing fixes, use multiple competing models to backport them to the versions in Ubuntu, and run automatic testing on them. Then a different group of "judging models" will evaluate the fixes and look for consensus. When candidates are chosen, they pass through normal Ubuntu package testing. If there are edge cases, low confidence scores, deadlocks, or other problems, then the process will be escalated to the staff of Canonical's security team.

It's an attempt, as Guillemin put it, "to use AI to fight AI" – cooperating groups of LLMs patching their way through the ever-increasing flow of security holes. Even so, this is a remarkably courageous tactic (at the risk of using a famous British euphemism).

It's an opt-in feature of Ubuntu Pro, Canonical's security and support subscription – although as we reported in 2022, Pro also has a free tier, so security researchers and the community can try Edge out, study it, and report their findings.

We do sympathize with companies struggling against a rising tide of bot-powered security hole discovery. In theory, corporate funding can pay for faster fixes than a volunteer community can offer, but even for commercial vendors these are testing times. As we reported when Debian turned 30, surveys suggest that Ubuntu is about a third of the world Linux user base. Some of those users will be intrepid enough to try this, and that will end up being informative for the whole FOSS world.

Those with long memories will remember the last time Canonical used the same edgy nomenclature. Back in July 2013, it launched a crowdfunding campaign for an Ubuntu smartphone. The campaign didn't raise enough money. ®

38e687e355221e94: Microsoft has released an out-of-band update to fix licensing and activation errors introduced by November's Windows security update.

The fix is available from the Microsoft Update Catalog for Windows Server 2025, 2022, and 2019, Windows 10 22H2 ESU, and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021 and 2019. Windows 11 23H2 users can obtain it from the Catalog or through Windows Update's Optional updates menu.

The "non-security OOB update" targets affected enterprise devices. Microsoft stated: "Certain Windows licensing and activation operations using the Software Licensing Management Tool (SLMGR) might fail with error 0x80041008 (Invalid parameter).
"This primarily affects organizations using slmgr.vbs commands or automated processes to configure Key Management Service (KMS) activation, install product keys, or manage Windows licensing."
Devices that are already activated will remain activated, Microsoft said.

Breaking the machinery customers use to activate paid-for software is a bad look for a Patch Tuesday release. Administrators may wonder how Microsoft's updates are tested when installing one means waiting for another to repair the damage.
Those same administrators may also have been fielding calls about last week's widespread Exchange Online outage, which Microsoft has partly attributed to a defect it introduced in July.

On top of that, Microsoft told administrators just days ago to consider unsupported Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 "permanently vulnerable." Exchange Online avoids that particular support deadline, but the recent outage was a reminder that handing over the servers doesn't make software defects disappear.
Forget "security by obscurity." Last week's approach was more like "security by unavailability."
Between getting Windows activated and keeping Exchange Online online, Microsoft gave administrators plenty to do. None of it was likely to feature in their original plans for the week.
Not all the glitches introduced by November's Patch Tuesday have yet been resolved, as some customers using a Windows device to print will be aware. ®
24c11abe66a97610: LearnWorlds, a software and learning course platform, says an attacker sent 13,000 phishing emails to customers over seven days by using automated tools to open free trial accounts. The company insists its systems were not breached.

Panos Siozos, Co-founder and CEO at LearnWorlds, said the miscreant created around 570 free trial accounts on the platform between November 7-14, which they used to issue fake copyright infringement notices to customers.
"We have found no evidence of unauthorized access to existing customer schools or personal data held for our customers and their end users," he told The Register.
According to Siozos, the attacker bypassed the platform's per-customer limit on trial subscriptions and exploited its welcome email feature to send the phishing emails.

"In each trial they added their own list of target addresses and rewrote the standard welcome email as a fake copyright notice," he said. "Adding those users triggered the welcome email from our sending address."

The first email was sent on November 7, after which the company detected the suspicious signups and blocked the first sender on November 9, although the attacker returned to send a second wave of emails within 40 minutes.
LearnWorlds removed all the trial accounts by November 10 and one paid account, which was used to launch more emails, on November 14.

"In total, around 13,000 emails were sent to addresses on external recipient lists supplied by the sender," said Siozos. "The trial accounts sent 9,853 between November 7-9, and the paid account sent 3,723 on November 14.
"We can’t tell how many people clicked, because the link was disguised to hide clicks. The recipient addresses were the sender’s own list."
The CEO confirmed that LearnWorlds has since enhanced its bot checks and is placing holds on new accounts if their emails trigger fraud flags.

"We have also examined the novel patterns the attackers used to create more advanced scoring mechanisms. We have reported the phishing website so it can be taken down. Further measures are currently being examined.
"Anyone who signed in on the fake page should change their Google password and review their account’s recent security activity."

The company's confirmation follows suspicions of foul play aired by users on social media. User reports included copies of the emails they received, which demanded urgent responses to fake copyright infringement claims related to YouTube content.
Among the more prominent recipients of the copyright infringement email notices was Marcus Hutchins, of WannaCry fame, who claimed he received an email from the company’s official mail server.

The email, a copy of which Hutchins posted to X, referenced general intellectual property and copyright infringements but failed to specify any specific issues. The email prompted the recipient to click a YouTube link to see the “supporting documentation submitted by LearnWorks.”

The link predictably turned out to be a YouTube redirect link, taking recipients to a separate website that presents them with a real Google OAuth page. If the user completed the authorization flow, it would have handed attackers control of the target’s Google and YouTube accounts.

“The site is designed to look like an official YouTube webpage that enables users to review copyright claims against their channel,” Hutchins wrote. “It contains both the YouTube and Google branding, as well as a very similar theme to the official YouTube one.”

According to Hutchins' screenshots, and those posted by others, the attacker was actively tweaking the email style and format, although the underlying lure and authentication mechanisms remained the same.
Hutchins didn't specify exactly how the phishing page steals access to targets’ Google accounts, although his description aligns with the steps often seen in OAuth consent phishing attacks.

These involve malicious websites serving victims genuine OAuth pages, into which unwitting victims enter their credentials and pass the relevant MFA tests. Typical scenarios see permission pages appear immediately after, and if the user accepts, the malicious website is handed OAuth access tokens to the victim’s account, effectively the keys to control it.

LearnWorlds, based in Cyprus, claims to have two million active monthly learners on its platform accessing 900,000 courses and more than 14,000 business customers. Since launching in 2014, it claims to have generated more than $1 billion in revenue.

The business focuses on white-label courses - training programs developed by one business and sold to another, assuming the buyer will change the branding and present the course materials as their own. ®

0ae7983049f12656: Nine countries including the UK have signed a US declaration pledging to secure supply chains for AI tech, as pressure grows for tighter export controls following the high-profile resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

The US is firming up its Pax Silica initiative on AI and supply chain security. Under the San Francisco declaration, signed on November 15, the coalition says it is entering a new phase that turns shared principles into a working partnership with shared responsibilities.

Pax Silica was announced in December last year, ostensibly for the participants to work together on vital parts of the global technology supply chain, including frontier foundation models, compute and semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, minerals refining and processing, and energy.

But the list of participants was notable for not including one country – China – leading many to suspect that Pax Silica is yet another effort by Washington to squeeze out its main rival in the global technology and economic stakes. Hong-Kong based South China Morning Post refers to it as Trump's "campaign to China-proof AI and chip supply chains."

The latest declaration states that "the security of our peoples cannot be separated from the security of our economies and those of our closest partners," and sets out what must be protected, as well as committing to "protect it together."
It asserts that protection should cover key foundational technologies essential to economic security, listing "software, materials, knowledge, components and inputs…essential to AI supply chains."

This includes anything that "theft, illicit transfer, or acquisition by hostile actors would confer a meaningful military or intelligence advantage, or undue economic leverage over the participants, or whose unauthorized transfer or misuse could pose significant risks to the economic and national security of the participants."
Also listed is the protection of critical infrastructure such as ports, terminals, transport, communications, and logistics networks, and the ICT and energy infrastructure these depend upon.
The declaration was jointly released by the US administration, and the governments of Australia, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Singapore, United Arab Emirates, and the United Kingdom.

"The know-how to design a chip, the machine that makes it, and the port that ships it can all be in different countries," the US under-secretary of state for economic affairs Jacob Helberg told the Financial Times.
"What makes the San Francisco Declaration historic is that Pax Silica partners have agreed to treat the security of those technologies and the infrastructure behind them as a shared responsibility."
This move comes amid reports that both Republican and Democrat lawmakers want to push through further measures to prevent China from accessing advanced chips for AI processing.

It follows the recent news that Jensen Huang, the now former CEO of top GPU maker Nvidia, admitted to an affair with a woman suspected by the US of being a spy for Beijing. She worked for a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed that bought Nvidia hardware and was also suspected of making it available to Chinese users. US, Singaporean, and Malaysian police investigations are still probing whether chips were diverted or accessed remotely by Chinese firms.
American efforts to control Chinese access to its technology started under the first Trump administration, and continued under President Joe Biden’s leadership.
A report out last week claimed US export controls are not stopping AI labs in China from using restricted Nvidia chips, and many of their cutting-edge models were trained using Blackwell GPUs.
It is understood that President Trump is to meet with China's premier Xi Jinping this week for bilateral talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. ®

b2955c38ff71d9a1: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors.

For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses.

AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built.

We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence.
Where traditional definitions of trust fall short

Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside.

Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox.

With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned.

Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event.
Building trust that scales

It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest.

Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture. The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark.

The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted. It means trust needs a different architecture. Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable. An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription. An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds. An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do.
Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter. Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions:
What authority does AI have? Define not only what it can do but what it is allowed to do, separating interpretation, recommendation, decision, and execution.
Is the function of AI proportional to the consequence? A marketing copilot and AI controlling industrial equipment need different assurance thresholds.

Are we taking the appropriate steps toward autonomy? For example, there needs to be a plan to move from having AI interpret while humans decide, to AI making recommendations, to then taking action with approval, and ultimately to having supervised autonomy, but only as AI can safely work at each step.
Are we testing the system or merely the model? Unexpected interactions emerge among models, data, agents, APIs, and human workflows.
Are we continuously earning trust? Monitor drift, failures, near-misses, and model changes throughout the lifecycle.

The winners in AI will be those who solve the determinism paradox—giving AI enough freedom to create value while engineering boundaries strong enough to make what it does with that freedom trustworthy. Invention earns attention. Trust earns adoption.

bbbda7c9a3961001: October ’26 might be remembered as a seminal moment for software developers and application security teams. AI agents are investigating unfamiliar systems, testing ways to get in and adjusting their next move when an attempt fails. Anyone with a credit card can use that capability to come after your application.

Coding agents and their tool integrations have introduced new entry points and surface areas that can be exploited. Pillar’s OpenCode disclosure in October showed how a malicious Model Context Protocol (MCP) server could execute commands on a developer’s Windows or WSL machine during authentication. A server-supplied URL reached a shell without tricking the model. In the same month, the discovery of the two PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, remote code execution bugs in the PHP runtime uncovered with the help of OpenAI’s models, brought new urgency to securing longstanding code across much of the internet.

Microsoft revealed that an agent moved from searching GitHub for exposed credentials to stealing Azure Key Vault data in five minutes. When its cloud API requests failed, the agent corrected the API versions and tried again until they succeeded.

A report by Anthropic described individual operators using agent frameworks for multi-victim campaigns that previously required specialist teams. Agents carried out reconnaissance, exploitation and data theft across targets in parallel, making sophisticated operations accessible with less hands-on work.

In a recent analysis, Tomasz Tunguz estimated the model cost of a 100-million-token attack workload using GLM-5.3, a low-cost model: 100 million tokens × $0.902 per million = $90.20. That is roughly 98% to 99% below the $5,000 to $10,000 frontier-model estimate cited by Bank for International Settlements (BIS) for a comparable cyber attack. Tunguz’s figure covers model usage only, not the full cost of an attack. Even still, it shows how trivially cheap it is now for attackers to go after any codebase, with the spend falling from thousands of dollars to under $100.

These new agentic attacks should make every team take another look at the code they’ve been running for years. Engineering and security teams need to find and fix weaknesses in their own applications before an attacker with an army of AI agents gets there first.
Security has to become every developer’s responsibility

Traditional AppSec checks such as rule-based static analysis, dependency scanning and secret detection are no longer enough on their own. Developers, engineering leaders, and security teams also need defensive AI agents that trace attack paths, uncover missing safeguards and business-logic vulnerabilities, and help fix them.

Developers’ responsibility doesn’t stop at the code they’re writing now. An application already in production without known vulnerabilities might still get exploited by an AI agent looking for ways to skip a permission check or business rule. The gap only shows up when a request is traced through the codebase and checked against what users should be allowed to do.
A new approach to securing your code

CodeRabbit Secure uses semantic analysis to understand your codebase and reason about it the way a security engineer would, tracing requests and checking whether permissions and business rules are enforced. Agents investigate potential attack paths and verify findings independent of the developer or agent that wrote the code, while CodeRabbit Agent generates reviewable fixes.

Deep Scan examines the repository, including older paths outside the latest PR. Agents map entry points, access controls, and sensitive operations, then investigate across functions and files. Linked repositories, when configured, supply context from shared services and libraries. A separate agent challenges each suspected vulnerability, checking reachability, exploitation conditions, and safeguards that could disprove it.

Recheck code as it evolves and validate findings at runtime

Each Deep Scan builds an attack surface map of the repository, showing which security-relevant entry points have been verified, which have gone stale as the code changed, and which have never been examined. Connecting the vulnerability finding, its supporting evidence, and a proposed fix helps engineering and security teams act while the context is still fresh and carry the change through review, testing and release. Teams can use CodeRabbit Agent to act on that context or easily hand it off to your preferred coding agent with a shareable markdown file.
What a million-dollar initiative surfaced

CodeRabbit recently committed up to $1 million in free Deep Scans to help organizations find and fix hidden vulnerabilities. More than 10,000 findings have already been fixed, including 1,049 rated High or Critical.

As agents produce more code and attackers become more capable, investigation using semantic analysis needs to become a regular part of how software is built and maintained, alongside existing security checks.

9af9c51a7fd2f67a: From Abd Rahim Romle and Ainur Rabiyatul Abd Rahim

A Malaysian applying for a licence, renewing a permit, or seeking government assistance should not have to navigate several websites, remember multiple passwords, or repeatedly submit the same information. Yet for some, accessing public services can still feel more complicated than it should.
We have become good at introducing digital platforms. The more important question is whether these platforms are making life easier for the rakyat.

Malaysia's digital transformation has brought improvements to public administration. Online apps, electronic payments, and digital records have reduced the need for physical visits and made many services more convenient.
These achievements deserve recognition. However, digital progress should not be measured simply by the number of apps launched or systems developed.
A government service is only successful when people can use it easily, reliably, and without unnecessary frustration.

Consider a small business owner applying for an operating licence. The application may be available online, but if the process still requires repeated document submissions, unclear approvals, or visits to different departments, digitalisation has merely changed the location of the bureaucracy.
The same applies to a parent seeking educational assistance, or an elderly person accessing healthcare services.
For these Malaysians, convenience matters more than the technology behind the system.

The 13th Malaysia Plan (2026-2030) places digital transformation and public service efficiency among Malaysia's development priorities. The challenge is ensuring that these ambitions translate into improvements that citizens can experience.

One persistent concern is fragmentation. Different agencies may operate separate systems with different registration requirements, procedures and user interfaces. While each platform may serve an administrative purpose, the combined experience can become confusing.
Citizens should not have to understand the organisational structure of government simply to obtain a service.

A more effective approach would focus on integrating services around people's needs. For example, starting a small business involves several administrative requirements. Instead of expecting entrepreneurs to navigate multiple agencies independently, government systems should provide clearer guidance and better coordination.
Similarly, families applying for assistance should not repeatedly provide information already held by public institutions, subject to appropriate privacy safeguards.

Another challenge is digital inclusion. Not every Malaysian has reliable internet access, the latest smartphone, or sufficient digital literacy to navigate complicated applications. Older citizens, rural communities, and people with disabilities may face additional difficulties.
Digital transformation should, therefore, preserve accessible alternatives while improving online services.

Three priorities deserve attention. First, government agencies should evaluate digital platforms through citizen experience rather than technological output. Processing times, successful applications, accessibility, and complaint resolution should become central performance indicators.

Second, greater emphasis should be placed on interoperability and administrative simplification. Agencies must improve information-sharing and eliminate unnecessary procedures before transferring them online.

Third, public servants should receive continuous training to provide responsive assistance across both digital and physical service channels. Technology cannot compensate for unclear procedures, weak coordination, or poor communication.

Importantly, public feedback must play a stronger role in evaluating service quality. When citizens report difficulties, their experiences should inform system improvements rather than disappear into administrative complaint channels.

Malaysia does not necessarily need another app whenever a service problem emerges. Sometimes, improving an existing platform, simplifying a form, or ensuring that someone answers a telephone call would make a greater difference. The objective should never be digitalisation for its own sake.

Malaysia's ambition to become a competitive digital economy depends partly on building public institutions that are efficient, trustworthy and responsive. A well-designed digital government should save citizens time, reduce costs, and make essential services easier to access.

The rakyat do not judge government efficiency by how many digital platforms exist. They judge it by whether applications are processed promptly, information is clear, and problems are resolved without unnecessary obstacles.
Malaysia's next public sector breakthrough may not require another digital platform. It may simply require making the services we already have work better for everyone.

Abd Rahim Romle is an associate professor and deputy dean at the Ghazali Shafie Graduate School of Government at Universiti Utara Malaysia. Ainur Rabiyatul Abd Rahim is a Master of Teaching English as a Second Language candidate at Universiti Putra Malaysia.

81186c1a62923f38: The contact details of 22 million people were accessed after a cyberattack on a subsidiary of France's postal service, officials say.

La Poste confirmed to The Register that an attack in September had resulted in full names and postal addresses being stolen by cybercriminals.The attack targeted the systems of Maileva, a business mail platform that's part of Docaposte, the digital services arm of La Poste.
Customers use Maileva for hybrid post services. They upload the documents they need to send to Maileva, which then prints and posts the letters on behalf of the customer.
According to Maileva itself, the service has more than 70,000 registered users and is trusted to send more than 180 million documents per year.
The digital assault was first reported by French cyberattack-tracking website Cyberattaque late last week, revealing that Maileva notified customers of an attempted intrusion in late September.
The letters mentioned the cybercriminal attempting to send emails using customers' official, trusted addresses, a situation which resulted in Maileva service disruption for six days.
A number of Maileva customers issued public statements confirming the attack in October.

Cornouaille's occupational health and safety service, for example, said the attack targeted Maileva's tracking database. It went on to say that senders' usernames and email addresses were also compromised, and that recipients' genders were exposed too, adding to the potentially affected data types that La Poste confirmed over the weekend.
Maileva told the organization it was not aware of any compromise of documents uploaded to the platform, nor did the attacker alter or destroy any data.
However, the disclosures of other customers suggested that each may have been affected differently.

In the case of the Foch hospital in Suresnes, whose debt recovery partner Kiwee was a Maileva customer, the names of documents sent to recipients may have been exposed, which may have indirectly revealed details about medical conditions.

According to Cyberattaque, the attacker also potentially accessed the contents of payment reminder letters, which in turn revealed additional details such as invoice numbers and amounts, and treatment dates.
Another case involving social housing provider Flandre Opale Habitat reportedly exposed details from letters dating back ten years.

La Poste said in a statement to The Register: "All teams are working hard to provide the best possible support to Maileva's clients and remain committed to rigorously and professionally implementing the necessary measures to ensure the security of its own operations and those of its clients."
The attack on Maileva is the second major cyber-related disruption La Poste has handled in the space of a year.

On December 22, 2025, the organization fended off a DDoS attack, which went on to affect mail operations for days, including online parcel tracking and its banking arm’s online services, right at its busiest time of the year.
La Poste described the DDoS attack as "unprecedented in its scale and power," and while it had mostly subsided by December 24, the attackers restarted it in the early hours of New Year’s Day.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> When writer and musician Samantha Shokin noticed her cover of a public domain Bulgarian folk song had been copyright struck on YouTube, she assumed it would be easy to fix. It wasn’t. And trying to figure out what happened led her to discover an AI content mill that is running 500 slop-filled channels and abusing YouTube’s automated copyright detectors.
“Any human would agree with me that there’s something clearly wrong here that needs to be fixed, but I can’t get in touch with a human being,” Shokin said.
Shokin’s journey is a modern nightmare that highlights the ways AI can be weaponized against human creators, and the ways people fall through the cracks of big tech’s automated systems.

During the pandemic, Shokin recorded a 50 second version of the Bulgarian folk song ‘Bre Petrunko’ and uploaded it to SoundCloud, where it didn’t get much traction. Two years later, she uploaded it to YouTube and watched as her cover grew in popularity, gaining 125,000 views in four years.

Last summer, she noticed an uptick in comments on the video. Unbeknownst to Shokin, her version of “Bre Petruinko” had become popular among DJs and electronic artists and had been sampled in dozens of songs. Someone in the comments pointed her towards one of the more popular tracks. “I look up this video and it’s something that has millions of hits [...] and 30 seconds into this track I hear my own voice and I was utterly shocked. I didn’t know how to react,” she said (the video has more than 4 million views).

“The first thing that comes to mind is, ‘Oh my god, someone stole my voice and didn’t credit me,’” she said. Shokin said she talked to a lot of DJs and figured out how they’d gotten her voice. They’d purchased a pack of samples from a company called Loopmasters that was selling her version of “Bre Petruinko” as part of its “Folk Legends” set.

“I got in touch with the distributor and they were deeply apologetic. They were unaware that this had happened and they immediately tried to make right of the situation and granted me royalties on the sample pack,” Shokin said. “At that point, countless DJs and music producers had been using my voice for their own tracks, unbeknownst to me. At least I’m aware and at least I was making something off of it and I was satisfied with that. I didn’t love the way that it came about, but whatever, they tried to make right of the situation.”

But Shokin’s “Bre Petruinko” saga wasn’t over. Last month, she opened YouTube and noticed her original recording was gone. A company called Media Nov Records had issued a copyright strike against her song, and YouTube had taken it down.She thought it would be easy to get this reversed. It’s a public domain folk song and she had the original recordings and a history with a distributor. “If I just explain it to YouTube, they’ll understand,” she thought.

Media Nov Records advertises itself as a “distribution company” that that partners with artists to release their music on digital platforms. But a lot of its website focuses on rights management and copyright protection. “At Media Nov, we go above and beyond to safeguard your musical creations. Our comprehensive rights management system leverages cutting-edge technology and legal expertise to ensure you receive the royalties you deserve,” it said on its website.

YouTube uses automated systems to work through copyright claims. When someone files a claim against a video, the company tends to automatically approve it. The original uploader can file a “counterclaim,” where they argue that the video should stay up, or that it should not be demonetized.

Shokin filed two counterclaims, but neither worked. “It's unclear to us whether you have a valid reason for filing a counter notification, so we won't be able to honor your request,” YouTube said in its last denial. It told her to contact the copyright holder; in this case, it was a public domain song and so there was no actual “copyright holder,” just Media Nov, which was claiming to hold it.

“I tried emailing them,” she said. “I tried calling them. There doesn’t appear to be a working phone line. I got in touch with [Loopmaster, which was selling her recording]. They tried getting in touch. I’m being ignored by everybody, by YouTube, by this media company that, like, the website seems to be entirely AI-generated, and all I want is to talk to a human about this.”

Media Nov’s site boasted about its use of automated DMCA takedowns, YouTube content ID management, and AI-powered content recognition. “Our advanced AI identifies your music across platforms ensuring accurate tracking and protection,” it said. The company says it has been in existence since 1996, but Archive.org’s Wayback Machine doesn’t show much of a web presence until last year. Its website is basic and barebones.

The company has two addresses on its website. One is an apartment building in Los Angeles on Marina Del Rey. The other is the Black Church in Dublin, Ireland — a cathedral that’s been converted into an office space. The site listed a Los Angeles phone number that was busy every time 404 Media tried to call it.

According to corporate paperwork filed in Ireland and reviewed by 404 Media, Media Nov Records was founded a little more than a year ago. Its listed address is the Black Church in Ireland but both of its shareholders gave addresses in Turkey.

404 Media found four different YouTube pages managed by Media Nov Records. Each contained hundreds of videos — many with AI-generated art assets and music. The songs are sometimes cross posted between the different channels and are mostly looping electronic beats. Think low effort “lofi beats” knock offs. The art assets are footage of sports cars, anime girls, and AI-generated pictures of women. The songs are cross posted on multiple channels and often generate fewer than 100 views. Each also has few YouTube shorts that revolve around “random acts of kindness.” A Douyin (the Chinese version of TikTok) watermark is present in some of these videos.

For example, recent YouTube shorts on its flagship page include a basic beat playing over an AI-generated woman mopping the floor of a store while being berated by her AI-generated boss. Another features an AI-generated woman crying over a well, and a crew of men rescuing her child. One of its other pages looks like this:

Media Nov Records told 404 Media that it operates 500 of these channels and “works with various artists, content creators, and music partners.” The company did not initially return emails or phone calls from Shokin or Loopmaster, but responded to an email from 404 Media.

It said it would look into its copyright claim of Shokin’s track. “We remain willing to review the relevant ownership documentation, original audio files, and supporting evidence to investigate the copyright claim thoroughly. If an error is identified, we are committed to taking appropriate corrective action promptly,” it said.

After 404 Media requested comment, Media Nov Records responded to Shokin and asked her to provide “relevant documentation supporting her ownership of the recording, including original audio files, recording evidence, original publication dates, and any other supporting materials,” which is a wild request considering that it has nothing to do with her recording and does not own the copyright.

The company told 404 Media that Shokin and Loopmaster’s emails had gone to its spam folder. “Regarding ‘Bre Petrunko,’ we would like to clarify that the musical composition and arrangement rights associated with Philip Koutev’s work must be distinguished from the rights in any individual sound recording. Media Nov Records also holds certain rights relating to the relevant musical content,” the company told Shokin in an email reviewed by 404 Media.

“Bre Petrunko” is an old folk song with no known writer. It’s primarily sung and most performances of it do not use instruments. Philip Koutev is a Bulgarian composer who popularized a version of the song in 1963. He died in 1982 and the copyright for that particular version is held by the Smithsonian. There are also many other versions of the song on YouTube, some with millions of views.

“Recording your own cover or performance does not automatically establish ownership of the underlying composition or arrangement. Likewise, rights in the underlying musical work do not automatically establish ownership of your particular recording,” Media Nov said.

“It’s ironic that they’re in the copyright business,” Shokin said. “It’s not the arrangement that’s in question. It’s the voice and performance [...] they clearly have no clue what they’re talking about.”

It's unclear why Media Nov Records brought Koutev into the conversation. 404 Media asked which song or work in its catalog triggered the copyright notice against Shokin but Media Nov Records did not respond.

“That makes it really ridiculous,” Alfred Steiner, an artist and copyright lawyer, told 404 Media. “If it’s her voice and her playing instruments, what could she possibly be infringing if it’s a folk song from the 19th century?”

The situation between Shokin and Media Nov Records sounded odd to Steiner. “I've seen lots of providers where you say ‘I have the rights’ and basically say nothing more than that, and they put it back because they’re taking a risk now. They’re harming her. If they just put it back, they’re at no risk,” he said.

“It sounds, to me, like a small company — despite the fact that they represent or run 500 YouTube channels — that are understaffed and is using a lot of different tools, probably a lot of AI, to identify tracks that are ostensibly owned by its clients and then automatically filing takedown requests,” he said. “They’re probably taking down far more than they have the right to take down.”

Minutes after it sent Shokin an email asking for proof she’d recorded the song, Media Nov Records followed up in an email addressed to both 404 Media and Shokin. “Following our review, Media Nov Records has decided to retract the copyright removal request for Samantha Shokin’s video. We are taking this step because the video has not generated revenue or received views, and we do not consider maintaining the removal request necessary at this stage,” it said. “However, this decision does not constitute a waiver of any rights we may hold. We intend to initiate appropriate legal proceedings regarding the underlying copyright dispute.”
Around 24 hours later, Shokin’s original video was back up. A spokesperson for YouTube confirmed that it reinstated the video after the claimant withdrew their complaint.
“It sounds like they got scared and feel like this is not a battle worth fighting,” Shokin said after seeing the email from Media Nov Records.

“Submitting a takedown request for rights that you don’t have can subject you to liability which includes actual damages and costs and attorney’s fees,” Steiner told 404 Media. “Doing this on a slipshod, shotgun approach is inadvisable from my perspective. Of course, if all of the people you end up offending are small parties and don’t have the resources to respond through the court system, and you are a fly-by-night entity that is hard to pin down and nobody knows who you are [...] it can be difficult to get a remedy.”

Shokin said she felt vindicated but was unhappy that it took a journalist emailing Media Nov Records to get them to listen to her. “They got my emails and they got Loopmaster’s email and they were just ignoring it because they only decided to respond because they got scared that it’ll be bad press,” she said. “It’s just not great all around. The whole system is broken. It feels like a broken system.”

413220c7807ddb35: Most victims of last week's Microsoft outage lost access to their email, but 15 unlucky guests at a German hotel got a dose of chlorine when a warning about dangerous levels never reached staff.

The incident, first reported by German broadcaster WDR, happened on Friday at Hotel Ling Bao, part of the Phantasialand theme park in Brühl, Germany, where a malfunctioning automatic dosing system pumped too much chlorine into the swimming pool.

The hotel's monitoring system spotted the problem and emailed staff a warning about the excessive chlorine levels. Unfortunately, Microsoft's Outlook service was caught up in a global outage, meaning the warning never arrived.

Brühl Fire Department said the problem started when a technical fault caused the pool's dosing equipment to pump in more chlorine than it should have. Chlorine gas then escaped into the swimming area, leaving guests needing medical attention.

Paramedics checked over 15 people at the hotel, and five were taken to hospital. Four suffered minor injuries, while one was moderately injured and needed further treatment. The fire department sent about 40 personnel to the scene, and crews spent roughly two hours dealing with the incident.

The incident came as Microsoft was battling a major outage that began on Thursday, November 12, and dragged well into Friday. Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, and other Microsoft 365 services were knocked offline, leaving businesses unable to access email and documents. The disruption wasn't confined to office workers unable to check their inboxes, with hospitals, police forces, and government departments reporting problems accessing the Microsoft services they use for day-to-day operations.

Redmond has since blamed the outage on a bug introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade. It sat there until a later network change set it off, and the failures then spread across the company's infrastructure. Microsoft ruled out both cybercriminals and AI as culprits, and has issued the customary apology.
At Phantasialand, though, a broken inbox was the least of anyone's worries.

The chlorine dosing equipment went haywire independently of Microsoft's troubles, but the email warning staff about the problem apparently never arrived. Whether the hotel had a backup alarm, or anything capable of shutting off the chlorine supply automatically, remains unanswered.

Why a hotel would rely on Outlook to deliver warnings about dangerous chlorine levels is anyone's guess. Email can be delayed, filtered into spam, or simply disappear when Microsoft's infrastructure throws a tantrum, none of which is particularly helpful when you've got a pool with guests breathing in noxious gas. ®

6368ac2908033cb4: SAN FRANCISCO—When Ars first drove the new Mercedes-Benz CLA last year, the automaker also gave us a sneak preview of its next driver assist. Called Drive Assist Pro, it’s for collaborative partially assisted driving, and from the passenger seat at the time, the demo was impressive. Now the automaker is getting ready to start rolling out Drive Assist Pro to customers with cars running the new MB.OS operating system here in the US and in Germany, and it let us have some time behind the wheel.

While most automakers want a reputation for safety, Mercedes has long used passive and active technology to do so in its products. It was one of the first OEMs to introduce airbags, and a decade later started adding active safety systems like anti-lock brakes, electronic stability control, and adaptive cruise control. And so, by giving the car’s electronics the ability to control the brakes and throttle, we arrive at the first level of assisted driving—called “level 1” in automotive engineer-speak.

“Level 2” assisted driving, where the car also controls the steering as well as the acceleration and braking, got famous with Tesla Autopilot. But the first lane-keeping assists predate it by almost a decade in passenger cars, when Toyota introduced a system in 2004. The human driver behind the wheel is still in charge, responsible for situational awareness (and anything that arises from a lack thereof), with the idea that long drives become less tiring and a little more effortless when the car does the boring job of keeping a constant speed or a constant distance to the car ahead and between the white lines.
0c510f0e83b9b096: A suspected Russian-speaking operator used an AI agent to turn security patches into working exploits with no human in the loop – a first such occurrence, according to the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) – before ultimately stealing data from victim organizations.

Google documented this attack in its fourth-quarter 2026 AI threat tracker, and said it marks a significant advance in how attackers use LLMs for fully autonomous vulnerability discovery and exploitation compared to Q3.

In this case, the threat hunters found an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework that integrates with multiple frontier and local models. The framework, called exploit_agent, used Russian-language tooling, and was configured to conduct continuous differential analysis of “popular web application software,” according to the report.
This includes comparing code before and after security updates, identifying potential vulnerabilities, developing exploits, and then automatically executing them without any human involvement.

The server also contained data stolen from victim organizations, and “multiple” post-compromise scripts that allowed attackers to perform nefarious activities including internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing webshells, and removing other attackers’ webshells.

“Victim telemetry on the server suggests the operator was specifically interested in targeting French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector,” according to the report.

The report also documents other instances of attackers moving beyond manual LLM prompting during cyberattacks and instead deploying autonomous, multi-agent offensive security frameworks to carry out multi-stage intrusions. These include both financially motivated cybercriminals and cyber-espionage groups.

In addition to the recent attacks involving the open source penetration-testing tool ARTEX, attackers have also used other AI-powered offensive frameworks, including CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, HexStrike AI, and PentAGI. In another instance, GTIG observed attackers using PentAGI alongside proxy services to target the aerospace sector.

“We have observed several threat actors separately experimenting with use of these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated, as well as suspected espionage threat actors with a PRC nexus,” the Googlers wrote. “Given the low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits, and massive scaling potential, we believe it is highly likely that threat actors will continue to use these frameworks in campaigns targeting organizations globally.” ®
e1b3eccce9b1092f: Celestial AI’s dream of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) at a distance will soon be a reality as part of a new collaboration between Marvell Technology and system integrator Penguin Solutions to build a photonic memory fabric.

Marvell acquired the underlying technology for the fabric from Celestial AI for $3.5 billion in February. It comprises a memory expansion module with two stacks of HBM3e totaling 72 GB along with support for eight channels of DDR5 stacked atop a silicon photonic interposer with 7.2 Tbps (900 GB/s) of bidirectional bandwidth.

“What we provide in this appliance is what we call a Photonic Fabric memory module… We provide these modules to Penguin, and they build the box, do all the power management, do the software, and all the management layer,” Preet Virk, senior VP of Marvell’s photonic fabric biz, tells El Reg.
Penguin’s first appliances based on the tech will support 16 of these memory modules for up to 16 TB of DDR5 and 1 TB of HBM, with future systems capable of scaling to twice the DDR5 capacity.

With 57.6 Tbps of bandwidth distributed via a Marvell-designed optical fiber shuffle, each appliance supports up to 16 servers either via a network interface card, or via co-packaged (CPO) or near-packaged optical (NPO) modules.

If you’re not familiar, CPO modules are typically integrated directly into the compute or switch ASIC, while NPO modules are a sort of half measure. They connect electrically to the host, whether that’s a CPU, GPU, or some other ASIC, and the rest of the fabric optically. NPO is expected to play a major role in the next generation of rack-scale systems from Nvidia and AMD, as it provides better serviceability and lower blast radius than baking photonic chiplets directly into CPUs or GPUs.

Through a software layer, which we’re told was developed by Penguin, each system can access the entire shared memory space, similar to how systems connecting to network-attached storage would have access to the appliance's full capacity.

As we understand it, a lot of this functionality is made possible today through CXL 3.1 compatible NICs and host CPUs, like AMD’s shiny new Venice CPUs. However, for NPO- and CPO-based memory, Virk tells us that CXL can be bypassed entirely.
The implications of this tech should be obvious. If memory can be shared and pooled across multiple servers, each of those servers doesn't need as much of its own DRAM, possibly saving some money.

In addition to facilitating communications, Virk says, the software also allows for several memory tiering modes by which customers can expose the resources to connected systems. For the most part, these follow typical CXL memory tiering conventions, with the exception of an HBM cache-through mode that Virk says will enable users to extract the performance of HBM with the capacity of DDR5.
This mode essentially treats the HBM as a read/write cache. Frequently accessed files are written to and read from HBM first before being pushed into standard DDR5 as they get stale.

Marvell and Penguin are positioning the new memory appliance as an alternative to storage-based key value (KV) cache offload. AI inference generates large KV caches, which are used to track model state across chat sessions, and long-running agents. Depending on the context length, these caches can be both computationally expensive to recompute and large to keep in memory.

Because of this, inactive KV caches are often offloaded to DRAM or flash memory, since it’s faster to store and copy them than to recompute them if and when a session is restored. Marvell contends that by offloading KV caches from HBM directly to these memory appliances, customers can achieve better performance and higher memory utilization.

Beyond AI-adjacent workloads, this technology also has potential to reduce the amount of DRAM required for individual systems, a concept we explored in greater depth earlier this year, and one that Meta has already embraced in its own datacenters.
Marvell expects Penguin’s first generation of Photonic Fabric memory expansion systems to arrive sometime in the second half of next year. ®
12604af31481c12b: Butterball Turkey Talk-Line experts take part in cooking and carving classes in 2009. AP Photo/M. Spencer GreenOne of the most quintessential American things is having roasted turkey on the table at a Thanksgiving feast. While that remains the norm, Americans are eating much less of this kind of poultry today than in the past. Annual consumption has fallen by more than 25% over the past three decades, while demand for chicken has soared. I’m a business school professor who has written about the economics of various holidays. I find turkeys fascinating, because even though I live in an urban area, a large group of wild turkeys has taken over my backyard. And I can offer several good explanations for the turkey slump. Receding since the late 1990s Domesticated turkeys, unlike their wild cousins, are a big business. More than US$5 billion worth of the birds were sold in 2025. That’s no chicken feed. However, it’s the latest sign of the industry’s decline. U.S. consumers are drifting away from eating turkey. Back in 1995, the average American consumed 17.7 pounds (8 kilograms) of turkey each year. By 2025, consumption had fallen to just 13.2 pounds (6 kg). While turkey consumption started to recede in the late 1990s, it began accelerating around 2008, when the Great Recession was underway. Occasionally, turkey production ticks upward a little, as happened in 2026 as demand for niche products like turkey jerky rose, but the long-term picture is one of steady decline. It’s not like Americans are eating less poultry overall. Chicken consumption has steadily grown during this turkey slump, rising about 50% from 69 pounds (31 kg) in 1995 to 104 pounds (47 kg) in 2025. In other words, we’re eating almost eight times more chicken than turkey. Well, at least the 95% of Americans who aren’t vegetarian or vegan are. More costly at every step in the supply chain Government agencies, researchers and some pundits have identified two possible explanations for why Americans are eating less turkey. First: pocketbook concerns. Turkey often costs more than chicken, except when it goes on sale just before Thanksgiving. Over the past 25 years, wholesale turkey prices per pound averaged about 10% higher than chicken, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data. That price, which is what big retailers typically pay, affects what you owe at checkout. For example, just before the 2026 Thanksgiving sales began, a Bell & Evans fresh whole turkey was going for $4.99 a pound, while a Bell & Evans fresh whole chicken cost $3.49 a pound at my local supermarket. That’s $1.50 a pound difference, which is significant in an economy where many people feel economically pinched. Nationally, you will see similar price differences, with fresh turkey being more expensive than fresh chicken. So, why is turkey pricier than chicken? Both turkeys and chickens are fed a diet of corn and soybeans. However, turkeys consume a higher percentage of soybeans. And soybeans currently cost about twice as much as corn. The latest data shows turkey feed costs are up almost 80%, without accounting for inflation, since 2000, while chicken feed costs have climbed only 60%. Too big for more families The second reason has to do with the size of today’s families. The typical Bell & Evans whole chicken my grocery store sells weighs approximately 4 pounds, while its fresh turkeys tend to range between 10 and 12 pounds. Big birds are handy if you have a lot of mouths to feed, but American families have shrunk over time. Today the average household includes only 2.5 people. The extra half-person does not represent children who are picky eaters or people who don’t like eating meat. It just means the typical family has between two and three people. That means cooking a 10-pound turkey results in 4 pounds of food per person, which is far more than almost anyone who is not a competitive food eater can consume. Cooking a 4-pound chicken, however, results in a more manageable 1.2 pounds of poultry per eater after getting rid of the bones, which make up about a quarter of a chicken. In simple terms, buying a whole chicken often results in one or two meals per person. Cooking a whole turkey often yields enough meat to produce meals for an entire week. Raymond Baker carves a turkey in 1948 while his wife and 16 kids surround him. Getty Images There are two more factors to consider. First, a 10-pound turkey costs a lot more than a 4-pound chicken. A 10-pound fresh bird at $4.99 a pound sets you back almost $50, while a $3.49-per-pound chicken that weighs 4 pounds costs under $14. Last, bigger birds take longer to roast. Cooking a 10-pound turkey in an oven takes about three hours, while a 4-pound chicken takes about two. That extra hour is a big burden in an increasingly time-pressed society. In case you were wondering, the world record for eating a turkey is held by Joey Chestnut. He gobbled down 9.35 pounds of turkey off the bone in 10 minutes in 2014. Please do not try that at home. What about wild turkeys? If you need to save money on turkey this holiday season, you should consider buying a frozen one. They are much cheaper. But can you save even more by going turkey hunting? Given all the large wild turkeys roosting in my backyard, I looked into what it would take. I live in Massachusetts, where hunting wild turkeys before Thanksgiving is legal. For much of the fall, hunters are allowed to use only bows and arrows. Beyond needing to be a proficient archer, they also have to purchase a sporting license, a turkey permit and an archery stamp for $95 each year. Having learned about that, I’m sticking to buying my turkeys in the supermarket. Jay L. 84377556b27b3648: The US Department of Energy (DoE) is deepening its relationship with HPC-first chip startup NextSilicon.

During Supercomputing 2026 in Chicago on Monday, the Israeli startup revealed that the agency had deployed its second Maverick-2 cluster in the Darwin testbed at Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL).

The deployment comes just six months after Sandia National Laboratories powered on NextSilicon’s first supercomputer, which features 64 nodes and 128 of the company's “runtime-configurable” accelerators.
NextSilicon’s latest DoE system is comparatively smaller, comprising just four accelerators, yet for LANL, the system is arguably more important despite its size.
Darwin, LANL’s chief scientist Galen Shipman, tells El Reg is a “long-lived testbed environment where we bring in newer technologies for evaluation.”
“It gives us the ability to work with the technology much more quickly, and integrate it with other components of our architecture in our environment,” he explained.

Smaller systems like the Maverick-2 cluster now deployed in Darwin allow LANL to validate and port a wider array of codebases to the chips, identify problems, and work with NextSilicon to not only address them, but directly influence the capabilities of future chips, Shipman explained.

In other words, Los Alamos’ interest in Maverick-2 is the first step toward larger scale deployments of NextSilicon silicon in future DoE supers. For this, hands-on access is kind of important as many of LANL’s most important workloads can’t exactly be run on public systems.
A compute chameleon

LANL is one of several labs tasked with ensuring that the US’ nuclear deterrent remains effective decades after underground testing was banned. The lab is also responsible for running simulations on energy sources like fuel candidates for future fusion reactors. Both of these workloads, Shipman tells us, fall into a category called multi-physics simulations.
These workloads aren’t really one workload, but multiple simulations that can have wildly different compute requirements.

A “good example is inertial confinement fusion. At the National Ignition Facility at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, you're using lasers to implode a fuel capsule, and the goal is to generate more energy through yield than you do from depositing energy to the capsule,” Shipman explained. “That's inherently multiphysics.”

There are simulations for the lasers, the hydrodynamics within the fuel capsule, and the chemistry and material interactions taking place during the fusion process. The problem, Shipman explains, is that a system that’s ideal for one of those simulations may not be well suited to others. “Identifying one specific platform that is optimal for that type of simulation is challenging.”

CPUs, he says, are well suited to workloads with large serial sections, irregular access patterns, and jobs that benefit from deep cache hierarchies. Meanwhile, GPUs are fantastic for dense, matrix-multiplication heavy workloads.

"Where NextSilicon fits in is being able to reconfigure to match the workload, on demand,” Shipman said. “The hope is that we won't have to make these rigid determinations upfront like, ‘we need this much CPU or we need this much GPU.’ We can use a much more adaptable, reconfigurable architecture to meet the workflow where it is at.”
A closer look at Maverick 2

Despite some visual similarities to Nvidia’s current crop of GPUs, Maverick-2 is not a GPU. Instead it employs a dataflow architecture which overlaps communication and computation. Rather than waiting for load-store operations to shuffle data around as you would with a conventional CPU or GPU, the chips themselves comprise a grid of arithmetic logic units (ALUs) which are configured to perform an operation like addition or multiplication in the order that they’re needed.
Data is computed as it moves from one ALU to the next, a bit like how a ball moves through a Rube Goldberg contraption.

This can make dataflow architectures extremely efficient in bandwidth-bound scenarios, which has implications not only for HPC and scientific computing but also for AI. It’s why we’re seeing dataflow accelerators, like Nvidia’s Groq, Cerebras’ WSE-3, and SambaNova’s SN50, being deployed as decode accelerators in AI inference clusters. Where NextSilicon stands out is that its designs, so far, have been specifically tailored toward sparse double-precision FP64 workloads.
Real FLOPS are rarely advertised

Programming dataflow architectures, historically, has been a challenging endeavor. To overcome this, NextSilicon claims to have developed a compiler that can decompose any existing C, Python, Fortran, or CUDA codebases into a graph that can run directly on its chips.

So far, NextSilicon has managed to validate its systems against the High Performance Conjugate Gradients (HPCG) benchmark, the LAMMPS molecular dynamics test suite, and the Sparta Monte Carlo simulation suite.

But as NextSilicon CEO Elad Raz notes, the roofline performance of Maverick-2 is different from one workload to another, and so the company has opted not to advertise peak theoretical performance the same way GPU vendors like Nvidia or AMD have traditionally done.

That’s not to say NextSilicon is shy about Maverick’s performance characteristics. Rather than advertising peak performance that the chip may not be able to hit in the workloads its customers actually care most about, it published performance figures across a swath of HPC benchmarks. For example, in HPCG, one of the closest watched HPC benchmarks after High Performance Linpack (HPL), NextSilicon says a single Maverick achieves 600 gigaFLOPS of performance, which it says is on par with contemporary GPUs but at half the power.
That’s just fine and dandy as far as Shipman is concerned. He tells us peak advertised performance is rarely a useful proxy for real-world performance.

“The thing that my team spends the most time on is how do we generate representative proxies, representative kernels; how do we generate specifications that communicate our needs to the broader ecosystem so that vendors like NextSilicon can meet us and co-design with us.” ®
