6f34bdccb710b683: Dave Maass has been writing about comics for more than 20 years, and now he also writes comics. By day, he teaches tech investigative techniques at the University of Nevada, Reno Reynolds School of Journalism and researches surveillance at the Electronic Frontier Foundation.

If I was the manager of a comic book store, I’d create a section for “journalism nerdcore.” It’s where I would stock Transmetropolitan, DMZ, and Abbott–comics that place fictional journalists in the center of genre stories, be it science fiction, action or horror. Despite their daylight jobs, Spider-Man and Superman wouldn’t be allowed there, but DC’s Lois Lane would find a home of her own.

On the end-of-shelf display, with a big fat, Sharpie-written “Employee Pick of 2026” sign: Exploit, the new comic series from Laura Hudson and Tim Leong and illustrator Emiliana Pinna, which was just published last month by Mad Cave Studios in its collected trade paperback volume. It doesn’t get more journalism nerdcore than its tag line: “Don’t Bury The Lede. Bury Your Enemies!”

Exploit is an action thriller inspired by the battle raging right now between the tech oligarchy and the independent press. Editorial intern Kirby Kuo is trying to score her first byline in RIOT!, a WIRED-style print magazine, before the newsroom is wiped out by its soon-to-be new owner, a thin-skinned Alex Karp-flavored cyberlibertarian-turned-technofascist. But when the subject of her reporting is assassinated on a live stream, Kirby finds herself facing the blame, on the run and forced to place her trust in agoraphobic hacker Lenox and Cold War-alum cybermercenary Ipsum.

Creators Hudson and Leong shared the masthead at WIRED (senior editor and director of digital design, respectively), but long before that they ran Comic Foundry, where they were “the team that changed comics journalism forever,” as ComicsBeat put it. Their careers have dovetailed between comics and journalism for years, with Hudson putting time at The Verge and ComicsAlliance and logging bylines in The Guardian, The New York Times, and Slate, and Leong holding creative roles at Fortune and Entertainment Weekly, while also writing and designing the Super Graphic series.

All that experience shows. Between the chase sequences and heist-planning, there are plot points based on real episodes in tech and cybersecurity uncovered in publications like 404 Media, WIRED, and The Markup. But the panels radiate with the earnest love for scrappy, independent journalism–especially print journalism–and a molten fury for those who threaten it.
I asked Hudson some questions to learn more about the heart and rage she poured into this series. The following has been edited for length and to avoid spoilers.
Dave Maass: Comics love an origin story. Take me through the back story of Exploit.

Laura Hudson: We've been working on Exploit since we met up in a diner in LA in 2019, pre-pandemic. I don't live in LA but I was there working on a TV show, and it was the first time we'd lived in the same city since mid-aughts New York. Tim fucking LOVES print, and we'd both spent the last decade watching print journalism collapse from the inside. There are definitely scenes in the comic, and a few darlings we had to cut, that were ripped directly from real life whether anyone believes us or not. We arrived just after the good times had ended, in time to hear all the stories about how amazing it had been, and watch it get worse and worse. And of course, the generation just after us only experiences the wreckage.

Tim had an idea for a comic set at a print magazine in New York, and I started imagining how I would feel, starting out as a journalist now. It always makes me think of donut blocks, from Super Mario Bros 3 on. They're the round, cakey-looking blocks in the game that start shaking when you step on them, and then fall down. So if you're going to walk across them, you better run, or you're gonna die. If you stop, you're gonna die. So, you can't stop. Ever. I understand that feeling intimately, and I knew I could write from there. And hell, I've wanted to make comics for over 30 years and now I'm finally doing it at 45? Fuck me.

Exploit’s main protagonist is a journalist (technically an intern) working for a magazine that specializes in tech investigations. It’s a WIRED meets Mother Jones kind of affair, but also if VICE’s Motherboard had been a standalone, hard-copy publication. Why choose a tech journalist as your hero?

It probably says something about me that this question baffles me. Maybe I've just known too many good tech journalists, because to me it feels so obvious. Technology and the internet have played, are playing, and will play transformative roles in our lives, often in ways that few people fully understand. We're still governed by a gerontocracy where many of our leaders conceptualize the internet as a bewildering series of tubes, possibly now filled with AI. Our technology has surpassed our ability to legislate it or address it ethically to such an extreme degree that some tech leaders are actually asking to be stopped. The internet (or at least its infrastructure) is a hyperobject in the Mortonian sense of the word, something so massive, complex and distributed that people struggle to comprehend it fully. We can see pieces of it, and effects of it, but it's impossible to perceive or experience it as a whole, even and especially when we are inside it.

But as Morton has written in reference to climate change, apocalyptic framing around hyperobjects can lead to hopelessness and inaction in situations when things genuinely can be addressed: "You are closing down the future. You are making your reader submit to tyrannical despair." Recognizing the enormity of something, in both the classic and popular sense, doesn't have to mean giving up. People who refuse to accept that something is too vast, too complicated, or too powerful to challenge are pretty compelling to me. That's what the best tech journalists do.

Now let’s talk about the dual villains–both techbro executives at a start-up that is not only a government contractor, but aims to take over key government functions. Now the last comparable comic I read like this was 2014’s Hacktivist (written by of all people actor Alyssa Milano with Jackson Lanzing and Collin Kelly), and it also featured two very similar tech bros–but they were the heroes, moonlighting as digital freedom fighters. That was a time where people were inspired by larger-than-life figures like Jack Dorsey and Elon Musk. That's not so much the case anymore. How would you say that Exploit’s antagonists reflect the shift in the public perception, and activities, of the “founder” class in our society?

We want to believe that there is someone coming to save us, and since billionaires were the ones powerful enough to fuck up human civilization, it makes sense that we'd look for someone of equal power to save us. It makes sense to want that. But this is a fairytale we tell ourselves, which I say as someone who once wanted to believe it was at least possible. But no one is coming to save us. Let me say it one more time, because this is important: NO ONE IS COMING TO SAVE US. Billionaires least of all. Tech billionaires, by and large, are much better at destroying than fixing, and have advertised this fact for decades. They like to move fast and break things, and leave them broken. Many of them struggle to understand human beings socially even as they run social networks. They are prone to massive ego, can have anything they want at any time, and exist in bubble worlds where they are never told no.

These are the people we're putting in charge of the future? I wouldn't put them in charge of a Dairy Queen. And I personally believe that some of them would be willing to accept the deaths of millions or even billions of people as the cost of advancing humanity in whatever sci-fi way they have imagined. Their obscene wealth requires them to exist at a scope that most humans are not built for, like images stretched out over miles. It distorts them as individuals, and it can distort their morality, insofar as it ever existed beyond the desire to advance and profit. This has become more evident as more tech leaders have chosen to behave as open buffoons in an age of buffoonery. But this is who they always were.

From the first pages of the book, we’re introduced to the very real, extreme asymmetrical conflict between tech billionaires. Even a poorly paid journalist can threaten a billionaire (or at least his ego), but a billionaire has so much money, it’s easy to crush a publication. It immediately made me think of Jeff Bezos buying the Washington Post, Peter Thiel bankrolling the attacks on Gawker, and cases where surveillance companies have threatened news outlets. Am I wrong to think that’s the overarching theme of the whole series?

Nope. I feel an anger about it so deep that I almost intuitively dissociate when it comes up. Not because I don't think I should be angry, but because I have learned I cannot be angry all the time without deleterious effects. Sometimes you just have to play the Yakety-Sax song in your head until the feeling passes, because you have to get things done today. It's worth noting that Kirby and Lenox (and Ipsum) [Note: Lenox is a young hacker and Ipsum is an old-school cybermercenary] undertake their mission with full knowledge that it will probably ruin their lives. That's part of the benefit package of being a billionaire. People can't challenge you without possibly ruining their lives.

Now Exploit isn’t meant to be a realistic treatment of tech journalism, but I do think there’s a lot of truth in how you portray the perils faced by journalists who deal with hackers and leakers. This is running in a publication that specializes in that, but a lot of other journalists have been burned pretty bad, some even ending up in jail. How did reality affect the way you handled the relationship between your protagonist and the various hackers who enter her orbit?

We've all seen things go very wrong for journalists, even those who meant well. Kirby has lived more life than the average intern, and done some journalistic work, but never at this level and never with these kinds of sources. She's green, and we wanted to show that. Before the big lead comes in, we have her pitching stories from sources that clearly have their own agenda, and her pitches get slapped down. That kind of pushback is essential, and what helps you learn before you're in a position to make serious mistakes. Kirby is pushed into a very big story before she is probably ready, but she's the only one in a position to do it. We wanted it to be clear that she's able to do what she does not just because she's smart and brave, but because she has an experienced group around her.

Dealing with hackers, leakers, and sensitive sources requires dealing with two competing impulses as a journalist. Good journalism requires rigorous skepticism as a discipline. There's that journo saying that if your mother says she loves you, check it out. But developing a relationship with a source requires trust on both sides, and risk on both sides. One of the things Kirby learns is that a source is not necessarily an ally, even when they have valuable information. Their goals may overlap in places, but they can be different in invisible and dangerous ways. It's not something anyone should approach lightly or without care.

A quarter of the way into the book, you introduce an assassination drone–and I initially expected it to be a sort of “Chekhov’s gun” that would play a huge role later on. But, it actually wasn’t. It turned out the most frightening thing still is people–specifically the mobs of doxxers who worship tech demagogues. Does this mirror your own experiences with online harassment?

One of the things people used to say a lot, to dismiss or ignore the nightmarish world of online harassment, is that it was "only" online. You could just close your computer and go outside, so really, wasn't it all in your head? This line of convenient fiction collapsed pretty quickly, as doxxing, swatting, stalking, assaulting, raping, and molesting people through the internet became, shall we say, super popular? You can't dismiss the internet as a fake, unreal place where nothing of consequence matters. We know it matters now, that it's dangerous. But now it almost feels too late to care. These systems and the people who run them have certainly shown they don't care, and there's no Band-Aid you can put on it now to fix it. We could have built the internet and its social architecture very differently, in a way that prioritized dialogue over the right to abuse. But the trolls thought it was funny, and the companies wanted more money, so here we are living in the cursed labyrinth of their lols.

One thing about an assassination drone, though: everyone understands it as a weapon. A tool of sorts, but one designed explicitly to cause damage. Its goals and impacts are not opaque. Social media platforms were pitched as a way to connect people, to give them the power to reach out and touch anyone from anywhere. Giving this power away to anyone who wanted it with little to no accountability was described by tech companies at the time as inherently good. It took longer—some would say too long—for everyone to realize the scope of the damage it could cause. Or that this incredible communications technology could double as a custom-made playground for grifters, bullies and predators of every stripe. So yeah, people are the scary part. But people get a lot scarier when they are given great power with zero accountability.

Zines play a major plot point in the book. But you also made a promotional zine for San Diego Comic-Con, which included a lot of digital security advice. How do you see physical media reemerging in political life?

Tim designed that, by the way, and I can't believe how much it looks like an actual riot grrrl zine. Zines have long been linked to comics culture, and you can see the overlap in a lot of indie comics spaces and events. But zines—or as they once called them, pamphlets—have been powerful political tools for over 500 years. They have defeated churches and kings. And they're a very compelling tool right now, as a form of dissent that exists outside of the internet and its platforms. You can't hack a printed page. And we don't think about it this way anymore, but writing on paper is a communications technology—perhaps the greatest in the history of the world—and we should regard it as such. A lot of obsolete or antiquated tech can have value today because accessibility is also vulnerability, and obsolescence is its own kind of security feature. There are some impressive Gen Z zine enthusiasts, and a great WIRED article about the scene. But I'd love to see more people pick up that torch, for both creative and political reasons. No one can stop you.
What do you hope people will take away from Exploit? How do you hope it will make them feel?

In the year of our Lord 2026, I would be happy just to give people a bit of distraction from the horrors. But if you feel like your life has been suffused by the feeling that you showed up after the party was over, and that it's only downhill from here, then we made this, in part, for you. It's a grim feeling we know well, a sort of miasmic dread that flattens the future and makes you feel helpless and paralyzed. And that's exactly how a lot of terrible people want you to feel. They want you to lie down and allow the terrible machine to function smoothly around you. Both Kirby and Lenox come up with their own imperfect coping mechanisms for that reality and feeling, but they do cope. They do move forward and fight, and they don't do it alone. They can't, and neither can we.

bf34b782a7d4f9ec: In Madagascar, biodiversity goals are being tested by funding challenges and local realities
Originally published on Global Voices
A booth at COP17 showcases Madagascar’s local communities and biodiversity. Photo by Sary nalain'ny mpanoratra. Used with permission.

At the 17th Conference of the Parties (COP17) on biological diversity, held October 19–30, 2026, in Yerevan, Armenia, Madagascar reaffirmed its commitment to protecting its remarkable biodiversity and showcased techniques local community members have implemented.

The country further outlined its plans and priorities for the future and promoted the initiatives it is committed to in order to protect both its terrestrial and marine ecosystems. This conference was also a strategic opportunity to strengthen green partnerships, develop new collaborations, and to engage with national and international stakeholders involved in biodiversity conservation.

To mark the occasion, Global Voices interviewed Tojotsara Ratefason, Director of the Directorate of Protected Areas, Renewable Natural Resources, and Ecosystems (DAPRNRE), part of the Madagascan government’s Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development (MEDD), at this conference. The interview focused on Madagascar’s role in implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the 30×30 global target, conservation funding, and the vital role of local communities, women, and young people in the sustainable protection of Madagascar’s natural heritage.
Watch the full interview in French here:
Raveloaritiana Mamisoa (RM): Where does Madagascar stand on implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework?

Tojotsara Ratefason (TF): Madagascar est confiante dans sa capacité à contribuer à l’atteinte de l’objectif mondial 30×30, aussi bien pour les écosystèmes terrestres que marins. Notre pays dispose déjà d’un système d’aires protégées qui constitue un socle essentiel pour préserver sa biodiversité exceptionnelle. Selon les chiffres que nous présentons, ce réseau compte 155 aires protégées terrestres et marines. Il s’agit d’un acquis important sur lequel nous pouvons nous appuyer pour poursuivre nos efforts de conservation.

Madagascar dispose d’un cadre national de référence pour orienter ses actions en faveur de la biodiversité : la Stratégie et le Plan d’Actions Nationaux pour la Biodiversité (SPANB). Ce document définit les grandes orientations du pays en matière de conservation, d’utilisation durable et de valorisation de son patrimoine naturel exceptionnel. Il s’inscrit dans le cadre de la Convention sur la diversité biologique, à laquelle Madagascar est partie, et constitue un instrument essentiel pour traduire les engagements internationaux en actions nationales.

Mais la protection de la biodiversité ne se résume pas au nombre d’aires protégées ni aux superficies concernées. Notre objectif est avant tout de préserver les écosystèmes, les espèces et les habitats naturels qui font la singularité de Madagascar. Notre patrimoine naturel est unique au monde et nous avons la responsabilité de le transmettre aux générations futures.

Cette ambition implique également de renforcer la collaboration avec les communautés locales (vahoaka eny ifotony), qui vivent au contact direct de ces ressources naturelles. Leur participation est indispensable, car la conservation ne peut pas reposer uniquement sur les décisions du gouvernement. Elle doit être portée conjointement par les institutions publiques, les gestionnaires des aires protégées et les populations qui vivent dans les territoires concernés.

Nous devons donc trouver les moyens de travailler ensemble, dans une démarche de responsabilité partagée. Les communautés locales doivent comprendre l’importance de la biodiversité, participer à sa protection et pouvoir constater les bénéfices qu’elles peuvent tirer de sa conservation.

C’est également dans cette perspective que le Ministère de l’Environnement et du Développement Durable cherche à promouvoir les emplois verts et les opportunités économiques liés à la biodiversité unique de Madagascar. Notre richesse naturelle ne doit pas seulement être considérée comme un patrimoine à protéger : elle peut aussi représenter une source de revenus et de développement pour les populations, à condition d’être valorisée de manière durable.

L’enjeu est de permettre aux communautés de mieux connaître la valeur de leurs ressources naturelles, d’en être fières et de comprendre qu’elles ont tout intérêt à les préserver. Lorsque les populations constatent que la conservation contribue à améliorer leurs conditions de vie, elles peuvent devenir des partenaires encore plus engagés dans la protection de leur environnement.

Tojotsara Ratefason (TF): Madagascar is confident in its ability to contribute to achieving the global 30×30 target, for both terrestrial and marine ecosystems. Our country already has a system of protected areas which forms the foundation for preserving its exceptional biodiversity. According the figures we are presenting, this network includes 155 terrestrial and marine protected areas. This is a significant achievement on which we can build to continue our conservation efforts.

Madagascar uses a national reference framework to guide its actions to support biodiversity — the National strategy and Action Plan for Biodiversity (SPANB). This document defines the country’s general direction in terms of conservation, sustainable use, and enhancing its remarkable natural heritage. It is part of the Convention on Biological Diversity, of which Madagascar is a signatory, and is an essential for translating international commitments into national actions.

However, the conservation of biodiversity is not limited to the number of protected areas, nor is that the sole area of concern. Above all our aim is to preserve the ecosystems, species, and natural habitats which are distinct to Madagascar. Our heritage is unique in the world and we have a responsibility to pass it on to future generations.

This ambition also requires collaboration with the local communities who live directly alongside these natural resources. Their involvement is indispensable as conservation cannot rest solely on the decisions of the government. Decisions must be jointly taken by state institutions, those who manage the protected areas and the populace of the regions concerned.

Therefore, we must find ways to work together and to share the burden. It is important that local communities understand the importance of biodiversity and participate in its protection and can see the benefits that they can raw from its conservation.

It is in this vein that the Ministry of the Environment and Sustainable Development is looking for ways to promote ‘green’ jobs and opportunities linked to Madagascar’s biodiversity. Our natural wealth should not only be seen as a heritage to be protected: It can also present a source of revenue and development for the population, as long as it is used in a sustainable way.

The challenge is allowing communities to better understand the value of their natural resources, to be proud of them and that it is in their interest to preserve them. Once populations realize that conservation can help improve their living conditions, they can become even more committed partners to protecting their environment.
RM: What finance is available for conservation and how is it used? And how does the government ensure that these resources actually benefit local communities?

TR: Madagascar dispose d’un atout majeur pour mobiliser des financements en faveur de la biodiversité : notre pays figure parmi les 17 pays mégadivers au monde, reconnus pour la richesse exceptionnelle de leur patrimoine naturel et l’importance de leurs espèces endémiques. Cette reconnaissance renforce l’importance de Madagascar dans les efforts internationaux de conservation de la biodiversité. Notre pays a également bénéficié de financements du Fonds pour l’environnement mondial (FEM), connu sous son sigle anglais GEF (Global Environment Facility), qui soutient des projets environnementaux.

Toutefois, au-delà de la mobilisation des ressources financières, notre objectif est de faire en sorte que ces financements puissent atteindre les communautés locales. Les populations vivant à proximité des aires protégées jouent un rôle essentiel dans la préservation des écosystèmes et doivent pouvoir bénéficier concrètement des efforts de conservation.

Nous devons donc veiller à ce que les financements consacrés à la biodiversité ne servent pas uniquement à soutenir les activités de protection de la nature, mais contribuent également au développement des communautés concernées. Il est important que les populations locales puissent tirer des bénéfices de la conservation, notamment à travers des initiatives économiques durables et des activités génératrices de revenus compatibles avec la préservation des ressources naturelles.

L’enjeu est de concilier la protection de notre patrimoine naturel avec l’amélioration des conditions de vie des populations. La conservation doit être une responsabilité partagée, mais aussi une opportunité pour les communautés locales. En constatant les bénéfices concrets de ces actions, elles pourront s’impliquer davantage dans la protection de la biodiversité malgache.

TR: Madagascar has a major advantage when it comes to securing funding for biodiversity. Our country is one of the world’s 17 megadiverse countries, recognized for the exceptional richness of their natural heritage and the importance of their endemic species. This recognition reinforces the importance of Madagascar in international efforts in biodiversity conservation. Our country also benefits from funding from the Global Environment Facility (GEF), which supports environmental projects.

At the same time, as well as mobilising financial resources our aim is to ensure that these funds reach local communities. Communities living near the protected areas play an essential role in preserving ecosystems and should receive concrete benefits for the conservation efforts.

We must, therefore, ensure that the funds allocated to biodiversity are not only used for nature conservation but that they also contribute to the development of local communities. It is important that these local communities can see the benefits of conservation particularly through sustainable economic initiatives and income-generating activities that are compatible with the preservation of natural resources.

The challenge is to reconcile protecting out natural heritage with the improvement in living conditions of these local communities. Conservation should be a shared responsibilty but also an opportunity for local people. By seeing the concrete benefits of these initiatives they will get more involved in protecting Madagascan biodiversity.

39994499436d36ce: Drawing upon Lord Denning’s advocacy of common sense in judicial decisions – alongside my own worldly and judicial experience in Malaysia, rooted in my origins in Thopputhurai, Vedaranyam, Tamil Nadu, India – I will state bluntly: no person operating in isolation possesses the capacity to defraud a nation on a scale that attracts universal infamy without the active assistance of a wider network.

When I sat as a judge, I treated common sense as my primary guiding principle when interpreting the Federal Constitution, the law and the facts of any case. It was strictly through this practical approach that I developed the oath of office jurisprudence as well as the concept of university-cum-court annexed arbitration.

With his 38-year career on the English bench, Denning earned the title of “the people’s judge”. At the heart of his jurisprudence was a simple, powerful conviction: the law is neither an abstract puzzle for academics nor a rigid trap for ordinary citizens.
Instead, he advocated, judges and lawyers must apply practical common sense to achieve real justice when interpreting both statutes and facts.
Among his many judgments grounded in common sense, I was particularly guided by his approach in Butler Machine Tool Co Ltd v Ex-Cell-O Corp (England) Ltd.

In resolving commercial contract disputes, Denning advocated looking at the entirety of the documents to determine what a sensible businessperson would understand, rather than applying rigid, artificial formulas.

Regarding the SRC International case, I have previously written that, among other critical issues, Najib Razak was deprived of procedural fairness and his constitutional right to counsel. Common sense dictates that procedural fairness is a core pillar of the criminal justice system and our constitutional framework.

Furthermore, it is a fallacy for certain commentators to circulate articles suggesting that a single Malay individual could orchestrate a massive fraud against the nation entirely on his own without the involvement of non-Malay enablers and professionals.

In my view, it is a travesty of justice to paint a picture suggesting that one person possessed the solitary capability to execute a grand-scale national scam without the active participation of accomplices across different communities.

7a98f561f849cd66: AI could help bridge educational inequality in a country where thousands of students still learn outdoors
Originally published on Global Voices
Photo taken by Rahul Ingle, May 2012. This file is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license.

In many communities across Mozambique, formal education still takes place in the open air, under trees, in improvised yards, or inside fragile structures that barely offer protection from the sun and rain. These so-called outdoor classrooms are not an innovative pedagogical choice, but more often than not, the expression of a structural deficiency: a lack of infrastructure, a shortage of materials, and an estimated deficit of around 12,000 teachers in 2025.

<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->During the rainy season (roughly November to March in Mozambique), the situation becomes more challenging. In several regions, the school calendar must be adjusted to respond to inclement weather, such as heavy rains that disrupt classes and hinder the continuity of teaching between November and March each year.

<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->In this context, the question arises: What is the place of artificial intelligence (AI) in an educational system that, in many areas of the country, is still fighting for the basics?<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->
A school without walls

In rural districts of provinces like Cabo Delgado, Nampula, and Zambézia, it is common to find classes of students studying under trees. The Minister of Education, Samaria Tovela, has been evaluating schedule adjustments because, while classes are frequently interrupted during the rainy season, concentration becomes a constant challenge during periods of intense heat. Without proper blackboards or textbooks, and often with a single teacher responsible for several classes, the learning process becomes irregular and deeply unequal when one million students learn to read and write on the ground.

<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->This scenario highlights a central problem: Learning depends on minimum standards that are not yet guaranteed in Mozambique. At the same time, one of the biggest obstacles to introducing technologies like AI in rural African contexts is the lack of connectivity. In Mozambique, about 73 percent of the population lacks internet access, according to 2024 data from the Ministry of Transport and Communications.

<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->Regional inequalities limit these initiatives, despite some progress recorded in recent years. This limitation directly affects the potential of solutions such as distance learning or digital learning platforms.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->
Language, culture, and the role of the state<!--TgQPHd|||[[2,[null,null,1,null,null,null,null,null,null,null,null,null,[351768,null,0]],[],null,1]]-->

Another critical challenge is the linguistic and cultural dimension. In Africa, where more than 2,000 languages are spoken, only a fraction — around 49 — are represented on digital platforms like Google’s translation service. Integrating Mozambique’s Indigenous languages, such as Emakhuwa, Xichangana, or Elomwe, into digital educational tools could significantly increase students’ comprehension and engagement, especially in the early years of schooling. However, implementing these solutions raises practical questions in contexts where access to technology is still limited.

<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->The overwhelming majority of the Mozambican population speaks a Bantu language most frequently at home (81.7 percent), and a portion cannot speak Portuguese at all (41.9 percent), though it is the sole official language of the country due to its colonial history. Despite this, the media, official government communications, and healthcare institutions continue to privilege Portuguese to the detriment of Bantu languages — the languages of the masses — which, activists argue, constitutes a form of social exclusion. Emerging initiatives, however, show that it is possible to bridge this gap with the aid of technology. In Johannesburg, for instance, tech startups are developing AI solutions tailored to African languages.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->
Risks and potential

Offline tools, pre-loaded content, and digital pedagogical assistants are some of the possible solutions to address the deficiencies and limitations of Mozambique’s education system. While the government does not yet have specific policies to integrate AI tools in schools, advocates say the state could play a central role in integrating technology into the daily lives of students and teachers. This also involves investing in teacher training; ensuring basic infrastructure; facilitating energy access; and strengthening partnerships with universities, startups, and international organizations.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->

Talking about artificial intelligence in outdoor classrooms may seem contradictory at first glance, but it is precisely in these contexts that technology needs to be considered creatively and responsibly, not as a replacement for the essential, but as a strategic complement.

The priority remains clear: Building schools, training teachers, and ensuring access to basic materials. The question is how to integrate developed technology without creating profound inequalities, respecting local contexts, and placing the student and teacher at the center of decision-making. In a country where learning still takes place under trees, the future of education will depend not only on the technology available, but also on the political and social choices that define who has access to knowledge and under what conditions.

088d1c55b762379a: <!--kg-card-begin: html-->
<!--kg-card-end: html--> Welcome back to the Abstract! These are the studies this week that watched movies, made sacrifices, got crafty, and aged backwards.

First, scientists learn how primates make meaning out of visuals by peeking into the brains of monkeys as they watch Despicable Me. Then: human sacrifice as climate “crisis rituals,” the fingerprints of prehistoric children, and the longevity secrets of ants.
As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files.
Humans watching monkeys watching Minions
Raghavan, Vinay S et al. “During natural vision, semantic novelty modulates fixation-related processing in primate cortex.” JNeurosci.

Settling down to watch a film is often viewed as a way to relax and shut our brains off for a while. Our brains, however, beg to differ—they are as busy as ever when interpreting videos, according to a new study based on brainwaves of humans and primates as they watch movies and short clips.

To better understand how primate brains make meaning out of visual scenes, researchers studied eye movements and electroencephalogram (EEG) readings of neural activity in dozens of humans, as well as two macaques, as they watched videos.

“Primate vision relies on eye movements to sample the world, yet how the brain integrates high level meaning across these ‘snapshots’ remains a mystery,” said researchers led by Vinay Raghavan of the City College of New York. The new results hint that “visual processing is not a series of independent glimpses, but a continuous process,” the team said.

Human participants with EEG electrodes attached to their scalps (the “scalp movie dataset”) watched a selection of films including The Big Sick, The Peanut Butter Falcon, Whiplash, Room, Me and Earl and the Dying Girl, The Tomorrow Man, Dom Hemingway, Life After Beth, Woodshock, and The Comedian.
“Participants were instructed to watch the movie as they would normally watch a movie,” the team said.

A different “intracranial dataset” included several human patients and two rhesus macaques, the latter of which had electrodes implanted inside their skulls. This group watched shorter videos, including 10-minute clips of Despicable Me in both English and Hungarian, a 4.3-minute clip of the short film The Present, and three 5-minute clips of documentaries featuring macaques.

Taken together, the datasets revealed that the brain responds to “semantic novelty”—meaning new semantic or conceptual information that crops up over the course of a video—which is measured through patterns of short-gaze “fixations.” The study also suggests that many brain regions beyond visual processing are involved in this ability to draw meaning from scenes.

“These results challenge traditional vision models that treat fixations as independent snapshots and highlight the importance of considering the temporal dynamics of eye movements and the predictive nature of visual processing,” the team concluded.

In addition to opening a new window into the mind, the study raises the irresistible yet unanswerable question of what macaques make of Minions. Alas, here we must confront the limitations of the knowable universe.
In other news…
Relatively peaceful—apart from the odd mass human sacrifice
Snyder, Thomas and Klaus, Haagen. “Pax Lambayeque? Trauma, interpersonal violence, and environment over 3,000 years in the Lambayeque Valley Complex, Peru.” Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

When climate-related disasters struck ancient Peru, some cultures responded with mass human sacrifices to appeal to the cosmos. For example, at least 107 adult men were sacrificed in six closely-timed events at Huaca de la Luna around 550–600 CE, and more than 140 children and 200 juvenile camelids were sacrificed at the Huanchaquito-las Llamas site around 1450 CE.

These ritualized killings often coincided with flooding and freak weather related to the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, the natural climate phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean that cycles through a warm “El Niño” phase and a cooler “La Niña” phase. The Huaca de la Luna sacrifice, for instance, occurred during a so-called “mega-Niño.” This connection inspired researchers to determine if environmental conditions were also linked to interpersonal violence outside of these ceremonial “crisis rituals” that were organized by elites.

The team conducted a meta-analysis of the skeletal remains of 1,633 individuals that lived in Peru’s Lambayeque Valley over the course of 3,000 years before the arrival of Europeans. The remains presented “no strong evidence for an association between environmental factors and interpersonal violence” and suggested “that non-ritual violence in the Lambayeque Valley Complex was rare (1.6%),” according to the study.

The mass sacrifices reflect “the sometimes lethal relationships between human behavior, cultural norms, and the environment—and are frequently used as cautionary allegories regarding the ongoing climate crisis,” said authors Thomas Snyder of New York University and Haagen Klaus of George Mason University.
Time to add “prevention of ritualized human sacrifice” to the list of reasons to address climate change. Worth a shot?
Before Play-Doh, there was clay-doh
Davin, Laurent et al. “Modelling symbols among the first-sedentary communities: Emergence of clay figurines in Epipaleolithic Southwest Asia.” PLOS One.

The fingerprints of children who lived 15,000 years ago in the southern Levant are preserved on clay artifacts, a discovery that exposes “a rare direct testimony of inter-generational knowledge transmission in a hands-on apprenticeship,” according to a new study.

Archaeologists studied 154 clay figurines that were unearthed across three archaeological sites in Israel, including a subset depicting birds, a gazelle, and two human forms. Crafted by the Natufian culture, these artifacts represent “the earliest evidence of a figurative clay tradition in Southwest Asia where it marks an important step in the evolution of human technology,” said researchers led by Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

Because these people sculpted the artifacts by hand, fingerprints are occasionally spotted on the clay, revealing the contributions of children and adults. In some cases, a preserved “succession of gestures on the wet clay suggests that, during the modeling sequence, an adult passed on the figurine to a pre-pubescent child,” the team said. “Therefore, these artefacts could be interpreted as portable figurative mnemotechnic devices related to children’s learning of traditional beliefs and ethno-ornithological knowledge.”

It’s so evocative to see the preserved touch of a child who lived so long ago, capturing a moment of skill-building and, perhaps, play. While we don’t know exactly what these figurines meant to their crafters, their survival is a testament to human creativity and imagination.
The ants are Benjamin-Buttoning
Cole, Blaine J. and Wiernasz, Diane C. “A replaceable soma enables negative senescence in harvester ants.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

We humans are used to a pretty standard life cycle: Birth, reproductive years, a decline in fertility, and an inevitable slide toward mortality. But a multi-decade study of ants reveals that some colonies operate as “superorganisms” that display increased reproduction and decreased mortality rate with age, reversing the course of normal senescence.

Researchers who gathered 34 years of data on 3,285 colonies of the western harvester ant (Pogonomyrmex occidentalis) discovered that these groups “display reverse aging,” according to their new study.

“We will show that colonies of P. occidentalis not only have extraordinary longevity, but that their pattern of aging differs dramatically from that of most insects,” said authors Blaine J. Cole and Diane C. Wiernasz of the University of Houston. “Colonies exhibit negative senescence—increased survival and reproduction with greater age.”

This finding does not mean that individual ants are aging in reverse; worker ants live and die normally in these colonies. However, the larger superorganism becomes an unusual “non-senescing form.” While the ants go marching one by one, the colony’s lifespan adds up to a larger sum.
Thanks for reading! See you next week.
037e089a5d550c90: Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice.

The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars.

Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It's what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets.

1422e3c7730e1566: The Trump administration’s blind eye to severe human rights violations in Azerbaijan is deadly for political prisoners
Originally published on Global Voices
Bahruz Samadov being brought to Sabail District Court in 2024. Image by Voice of America, via Wikimedia Commons. Public domain.

Bahruz Samadov is an Azerbaijani political scientist, peace activist, and PhD candidate at Charles University in Prague, or at least he was until the summer of 2024. On August 21, 2024, the State Security Service detained Samadov while he was visiting his grandmother in Baku. Global Voices reported on his arrest at the time, as part of a wider crackdown on critics before Azerbaijan hosted COP29 in November 2024.

Samadov was one of the few Azerbaijani voices to oppose the 2020 Karabakh war. In his writing for OC Media, Eurasianet and other outlets, he argued for dialogue with Armenia and criticized the expulsion of ethnic Armenians from Karabakh. Prosecutors charged him with high treason based on his WhatsApp exchanges with Armenian peace activists and on publicly available information. Samadov denied the charges and called himself a “prisoner of peace.” His lawyer argued that the prosecution’s theory of “indirect espionage” was vague and had no basis in case law.

On June 23, 2025, after a closed-door trial, the Baku Grave Crimes Court sentenced him to 15 years in prison. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld the verdict in September 2025, and the Supreme Court did the same in September 2026. Amnesty International, which considers him arbitrarily imprisoned, reports that he has been held in solitary confinement and denied medical care, and that he has twice attempted suicide, most recently in his Supreme Court hearing. Below, Global Voices publishes a letter Samadov wrote from prison and asked us to share.

The 2024 summer holidays ended in a nightmare: while visiting Baku, my home city, from my doctoral studies in Prague, I was detained by the notorious State Security Service of Azerbaijan and soon was charged with “high treason.”

Studying the ideological tenets of the hegemonic regime in my homeland, I directly connected its durability to the conflict between Azerbaijan and Armenia, revealing the narratives of “national unity” under the “savior strongman.”

During and after the outbreak of the 2020 War in Karabakh, I criticized the deployment of military means. Between 2021–2024, I partook in various conferences and meetings across Europe, presenting my perspective and calling for a meaningful and inclusive policy of peace and co-existence.

The Azerbaijani regime, having years of the crackdown experience, is aggressively intolerant to any kinds of contestation, and especially targets the independent academic voices. When the repressive machinery was re-launched in late 2023, the regime started the total crackdown on civil society, independent media, politicians, and academicians.

In private communications, more than five political prisoners connected it to the worsened relations with the Biden administration. The latter was highly critical to the human rights violations in Azerbaijan.

Weeks before leaving the White House, Blinken invited human rights defender Rufat Safarov to Washington to receive the Human Rights Defender Award. Several hours after visiting the US Embassy in Baku, Safarov was arrested and accused of hooliganism and fraud. It was an open signal to the US that the leaving administration had no power to endorse the Azerbaijani critical voices.

The Azerbaijani government acted differently with the Trump administration. The August 8, 2025 meeting and the peace agreement was the soon-disappeared sign of hope for us. Even if the peace agreement did not include any references to human rights, the current administration’s plans for the long-term involvement in the region brought hopes for at least minimal reforms in Azerbaijan.

Curiously, my sham trial was “fastened” and ended on June 23, 2025 — a process too explicitly controversial to the “peace agenda.” Following the US delegation’s visit to Baku in January 2026, a number of political prisoners, me among them, appealed to the US officials to raise the “political prisoners issue” to the official Baku — a policy that once partially worked during Obama’s second term.

However, the recent severe sentences and USA’s silence prove our call remained rather a mere cry from the chamber cells. The Baku-based team of Toplum TV, the veteran human rights defender Anar Mammadli and others have received up to 15 years of imprisonment. To compare, the EU Parliament recently adopted a resolution calling for the release of political prisoners in Azerbaijan. Similar calls were made by the PACE and even the UN.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration is proud to end the violence in the South Caucasus (by the way, this narrative is implicitly contested by the official Baku — there D. Trump remains a mere “witness.”) While the Administration of White House endorses officials like Hikmet Hajiyev for their nice compliments to D. Trump and villanization of “Biden–Blinken couple,” the sufferings of Azerbaijani imprisoned dissent keep going.

Many of those fellow political prisoners I had a chance to talk to remain pessimistic and sceptical regarding the US involvement in the region, dismissing the possibility of the “Belarusian scenario.” One prominent political prisoner even rejected to sign the aforementioned call: “They came for security-related issues, they do not care about human rights,” he shouted from the cell’s balcony. “We are Biden’s prisoners,” laughed my inmate, an imprisoned journalist and poet.

True, nothing publicly known has been made by the Trump administration related to severe human rights violations in Azerbaijan. If the Republican administration aspires to replace Russia in the long-term in the South Caucasus, it should not abandon the ideals of the Founding Fathers in the foreign policy standards. Washington has officially repeatedly mentioned the human rights violations in rival countries like Iran, Cuba, and formerly Venezuela. The selective attitude to the human rights issues and turning the blind eye to our suffering endangers the democratic security of the US itself, not to mention its international image. This policy raises questions about the adherence to the American ideals of the current administration.

Yet, it is still not too late to follow the recommendations of Amnesty International: “Use every available opportunity, in bilateral and multilateral forces, to raise concerns about Azerbaijan’s human rights record.”
Bahruz Samadov Umbaku Prison 27.10.2026

Samadov’s arrest and his continued imprisonment are clear examples of the breakdown in justice mechanisms within Azerbaijan. 9aba7fdcb091d85e: An order reissued by the Kuala Lumpur High Court led to two men packing their belongings and moving out — one out of prison, the other out of office.
The two are none other than former prime minister Najib Razak and now former transport minister Loke Siew Fook.

Now, Umno and maybe some PAS supporters are likely celebrating their “victory” — a conditional pardon for the former Umno president that sees him serving the remainder of his sentence under house arrest.
But can Umno really claim a “win” in this case?
If any party can hold its head up high in this affair, it certainly has to be Loke and DAP.
Loke stayed true to his principles, even if it cost him his ministerial post.
He vowed to resign if Najib set foot in the house and did not u-turn.
It is an admirable attribute, regardless of whatever side of the divide you are on.
Of all the adjectives available to describe Loke, Ahmad Zahid Hamidi chose “man of principle”, which must account for something, even if we were to doubt the deputy prime minister’s sincerity.

Loke’s resignation will help DAP recover its reputation as a principled party, especially among voters who have been disillusioned with them due to its partnership with Umno in the unity government and the administration’s delayed reforms.
Yes, being in bed with its most fiery rivals meant compromises had to be made for stability post-GE15, but the public doesn’t see it that way.
DAP, through Loke’s actions, may have also won over fence-sitters who are still angry with Najib and the 1MDB controversy.
Apart from these “wins”, unemployment may also work in Loke’s favour.
He now has the freedom to go to the ground to re-connect with the grassroots and members and he will be returning as a martyr of sorts.
Loke can now help revive the party in time for the 16th general election.
But what about Najib and Umno?
At the end of the day, Najib remains incarcerated — he only trades a jail cell for a comfortable home in Langgak Duta.
However, his movements, communication and personal contact remain restricted. To paraphrase a popular idiom: a cage by any other name reeks of imprisonment.
Secondly, Umno only managed to secure a conditional pardon and not a full one and helping Najib obtain a house arrest isn’t something one should boast about.
On top of that they had to help crowdfund RM50 million. Money that could have helped them win elections has been channeled to secure Najib’s house arrest.

Here’s the kicker. When the house arrest ends, he could head back to prison to serve his time for his 1MDB sentence, if he fails in his appeal. RM50 million would therefore end up being a hefty fee for a relatively short-term staycation.
Thirdly, Umno is now tasked with defending the indefensible and will have to do so with no moral ground to stand on, especially if they intend to play the religious card.

Umno, in this case, would have to answer for soliciting donations from people to help a convict who has yet to repent for his actions, which is religiously questionable and would likely haunt Umno in every election.
Umno’s friends and enemies will no doubt exploit this entire episode when jostling for seats during elections.
So. from where I stand, Loke and the DAP are the real winners here.
And all Umno has left is a house of cards.

4e02cf1dabde2b4a: A group of journalists and activists created ‘Verify This,’ a platform where users can find reliable information
Originally published on Global Voices
Screenshot of the Verify First website, ‘iVerify’, Armenia. Fair use.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Armenia is a small, landlocked country that has, for years, relied on Russian support in its long-term conflict with the neighboring oil-rich and authoritarian country, Azerbaijan. However, Armenia received a blow from Russia in 2022–2023, when it was not supported by Russian military forces during its conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.

In September 2023, Azerbaijan launched a large-scale military offensive, expelled the entire Armenian population from Nagorno-Karabakh, dissolved the government of the region, and incorporated the territory into Azerbaijan.

After this incident, when Russia did not support Armenia with its peacekeeping troops, likely because Vladimir Putin was already engaged in a full-scale invasion and war with Ukraine, Armenia visibly changed its attitude toward Russia.
Armenian Prime Minister ​Nikol Pashinyan started to work in earnest towards the goal of European Union ⁠membership for his South Caucasus country and increased diplomatic communication with the US.

He was re-elected on June 7, 2026. The election took place amid reports of Russian interference. Reuters, citing anonymous Western intelligence officials and documents, reported covert Russian efforts to undermine Pashinyan and support pro-Russian candidates, including through disinformation campaigns.

These elections showed how information warfare has expanded beyond social media. It now included fake news websites, AI-generated videos and material presented as reporting by reputable international media outlets.

According to the US-based disinformation monitoring organization NewsGuard, a Russia-linked campaign circulated 31 fabricated stories about Pashinyan in just one week. The stories accused him of election fraud and of trying to drag Armenia into a war with Russia.
Some of this material imitated international media outlets such as France 24 and Politico. Other stories impersonated Armenian news outlets, including Armenpress and CivilNet.

With the proliferation of generative AI, disinformation and propaganda campaigns have become increasingly sophisticated. Armenia’s experience shows how these campaigns operate in a country moving away from its longstanding reliance on Russia. At the same time, Armenian journalists and civil society are working hard to build media literacy to counter disinformation campaigns. This Digital Spark Spotlight interview is about one of these projects — “Verify First,” a platform where users can find reliable information.

Global Voices interviewed Armin Asryan, a member of the group of journalists, editors, and activists behind the media literacy project “Verify First,” which tackles Russian information manipulation and propaganda.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project.
Armin Asryan (AA): We are a group of enthusiasts, operating through the ‘Socio Club’ — Social and Information NGO — and dedicated to driving positive change in Armenia’s information landscape.

We chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project because we were thrilled to see an opportunity to actively contribute to a healthier, more reliable information space on social networks. In response to the growing challenges of online misinformation, we developed a targeted initiative to produce six educational video reels focused on practical fact-checking techniques and media literacy, designed to equip everyday social media users with the tools to spot and counter misleading content.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

AA: The Armenian social media space is heavily impacted by disinformation, low-quality content, and online hostility. Every day, social media feeds reveal content that not only disappoints users but also generates widespread panic and fear.

These unreliable narratives actively erode public trust in vital institutions. Recognizing that this negative information environment harms societal well-being, we felt compelled to act. This critical challenge prompted us to undertake our project, aiming to equip users with the critical thinking and fact-checking tools needed to counter misleading content and foster a healthier digital community.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?
AA: Our primary challenge was translating complex fact-checking concepts, such as lateral reading and AI artifact identification, into engaging, accessible content for ordinary social media users.

To achieve this, we focused on breaking down advanced media literacy techniques into simple, highly intuitive video reels. We designed our activities to ensure that even technologically non-advanced audiences could easily grasp and apply these verification tools. By stripping away heavy jargon and demonstrating practical, step-by-step digital hygiene habits, we empowered everyday viewers to independently spot disinformation, assess online sources critically, and navigate social media feeds with greater confidence and discernment.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

AA: This project was a mutual learning experience for our team and our community. Our target beneficiaries included adults aged 18 and older, with a strong focus on reaching audiences in regional villages. Witnessing their growth as they mastered practical fact-checking tools was deeply rewarding.

A key highlight of our impact was making this educational content fully accessible: we provided sign language translation for viewers with hearing impairments, ensuring that marginalized community members could benefit from our media literacy campaign. By bridging the digital and accessibility gaps, we helped foster a more informed, inclusive, and resilient public space across Armenia.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?
AA: We learned. We learned about fact-checking. We learned to be a group. It was a rewarding process. And we became aware that even little actions can have a big effect. We are very excited.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

AA: It was interesting. Two groups of content creators worked on the project. One team was composed of professional journalists over 60 years old. Another team was composed of young and inspired professionals in content creation in their early 20s and 30s. It was fascinating to see how experience could go hand in hand with young minds and innovation. The combination of older-age experience with the enthusiasm of the young was the lesson we learned from this project.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

AA: The video reels we created are not a one-time event. We are going to use them during training and also share them with other civic actors. But we also think that we should build on this. Right now, we have some inspiring ideas that we want to bring to life. Let’s see what the future brings.
Written by Daria Dergacheva

c3ab0a93475a80f4: Five city-run groceries in a city of 8 million won't substantially lower food prices, but the experiment might cause shoppers to think differently about the role of government. Spencer Platt/Getty ImagesNew York City is moving closer to launching its effort to counter food inflation by opening five city-run grocery stores. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026 that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow. Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with nearly 1,000 supermarkets and more than 8 million inhabitants. But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices. Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from independent grocers, supermarket trade associations and a coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses. What explains this pushback? As a food policy scholar, I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. Mamdani’s initiative challenges an entrenched expectation that the government should leave the provision of consumer goods to private enterprise even as it encourages businesses to invest in certain locations, regulates their activities and helps low-income shoppers through various food assistance programs. The reality is more complicated. For at least a century, New York’s food economy has not operated independently of government. In fact, public policies and investments have long shaped where supermarkets open, which businesses can operate with a profit, and how residents obtain food. It’s just that they have done so in ways consumers often don’t see. That is why the five grocery stores carry a broader significance, in my view. They offer a different model of public investment that makes the government much more visible in providing an essential service – and more accountable for its results. New Yorkers will get an opportunity to judge that contribution directly. If the stores succeed, they may change not just what people expect to pay for groceries, but what they expect their city government to provide. Some immigrant owners of New York grocery stores have warned that city-run alternatives will undercut them. Scott Gries/Getty Images How the plan will work New York City has committed US$70 million to develop these stores, which will be open to all. While they will be managed by private operators, the city will provide rent-free space, prioritize publicly owned sites and ensure that essential foods are priced 30% below typical retail prices. In this respect, the stores offer a “public option” – a government-provided good or service that exists alongside private alternatives, like public schools and city hospitals. Municipal grocery stores would offer New Yorkers a similar choice alongside private retailers. But as a public option, they would create a visible alternative against which shoppers can judge privately owned stores, setting a benchmark for food prices and service quality. They would also demonstrate how public investment can be used to make an essential good more affordable. At his May announcement, Mamdani described the proposed Bronx store and its surrounding development as “physical proof of our conviction that government can be a force for good.” A fresh form of intervention Government-supported food retailing has a long history in New York City despite opposition by existing businesses. In 1934, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia’s administration began selling discounted milk to low-income families, but the initiative drew complaints from grocers about unfair competition. Independent merchants similarly protested the city’s efforts to subsidize a new Pathmark supermarket in East Harlem in the 1990s, warning that it would put local grocers out of business. A more recent example is the city’s Food Retail Expansion to Support Health program, known as FRESH. Since 2009, it has offered supermarket developers and operators long-term tax breaks and zoning incentives to build or expand dozens of stores in underserved neighborhoods. These incentives have helped increase grocery retail space, but shoppers don’t see the public support behind them. FRESH is just one example of an approach toward supermarket financing that gained momentum in the 1990s, when governments sought to address social problems by encouraging private investment. Food insecurity was blamed on a scarcity of neighborhood supermarkets, not on prices being beyond reach for local shoppers. Subsidizing new stores promised better nutrition and economic development without confronting poverty or inequality, and FRESH reflects that approach. Participating supermarkets must devote space to perishable foods, but they’re not required to offer affordable prices. That may be one reason why researchers have found that adding supermarkets to low-income neighborhoods, by itself, doesn’t substantially improve residents’ diets. This hidden government role is hardly confined to grocery stores. Much of what government does for Americans is delivered indirectly, through tax credits, subsidies and private institutions. Because the public contribution is obscured, people often give credit to private markets for the benefits provided by public policy, from student loans to healthcare. This invisibility is a consequence of policy design and influences how citizens understand government, a phenomenon that political scientist Suzanne Mettler described as “the submerged state.” Bringing the state into the open Municipal grocery stores depart from the traditional model in two important ways. First, they make affordability an explicit condition of public investment rather than the outcome of increased retail competition. Second, they make government’s contribution visible. For example, the stores will share distinct branding so shoppers know who’s responsible for the affordable food. If the stores deliver reliable savings, shoppers may begin to see affordable food as something government can help provide, not an outcome determined entirely by private markets. When public benefits are obscured, people are more likely to underestimate government’s contribution to their lives. Visible programs, like a physical store in the neighborhood, make that contribution easier to notice and evaluate. Visibility also creates accountability. A customer at a private supermarket that received a tax break to expand isn’t likely to tie the store’s prices or food quality to government policy. At a municipal grocery store, with clear branding, the connection is unmistakable. To be sure, critics’ concerns deserve serious attention. Many independent grocery stores are owned by immigrant entrepreneurs operating on thin margins. Groups representing bodegas and independent supermarkets warn that a publicly subsidized competitor could draw away their customers. Some may lose business. Yet East Harlem’s Pathmark demonstrates that new supermarkets and smaller retailers can coexist. Between 2000 and 2015, the number of small grocery stores and bodegas in the neighborhood increased from 100 to 126, while supermarkets rose from 10 to 18. That said, those figures don’t establish Pathmark’s effects on individual businesses. The municipal stores’ impact on nearby retailers remains an open question. But the task for New York City is to ensure that private operators deliver excellent service and real savings, and that their commercial interests don’t undermine the public mission. It will also need to provide good working conditions and track effects on nearby businesses. Ultimately, public ownership doesn’t guarantee success. But it makes government’s responsibility for the outcome impossible to miss. Nevin Cohen receives research funding from the City of New York.

fa67c5920455837f: Microsoft products including Outlook were out of action globally on November 13 2026. Alex Photo Stock/ShutterstockWhen I arrived at work to discover that Outlook had vanished from my computer, I wondered how I was supposed to get through my working day. No emails. No calendar. No meeting invitations. Then another thought crossed my mind: when did we become so dependent on a single technology company that losing access to one application could disrupt our entire working routine? And what is the financial and environmental cost of that dependence? We regularly discuss sustainability in terms of reducing plastic, cutting carbon emissions and consuming less energy. But the digital systems we rely on every day also have huge environmental consequences. As world leaders gather at the UN climate summit, Cop31, in Turkey, perhaps it is time to ask an uncomfortable question: can our digital economy really become sustainable when so much of it depends on a handful of technology companies? The cloud has a physical footprint The cloud may sound weightless, but it runs on data centres, electricity, cooling systems and hardware. The International Energy Agency estimates that data centres consumed 415 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, around 1.5% of global demand. It projects that consumption could reach 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, largely driven by AI and other digital services. Microsoft’s own 2026 sustainability report illustrates the tension. The company reported a 25% year-over-year rise in total emissions in 2025, primarily because of expanding data centres and a change in renewable-energy certificate accounting. Microsoft is also investing in cleaner energy and more efficient infrastructure. Both facts matter: technological progress can reduce emissions per task, while growth pushes overall demand higher. Asking the right questions Turkey’s Cop31 presidency released the voluntary Antalya artificial intelligence pledge in October. This pledge aims to encourage climate-responsible AI while acknowledging the energy and water demands of the technology. The World Resources Institute, a global research organisation, welcomed the pledge’s direction but warned that voluntary commitments need stronger accountability mechanisms. Meanwhile, the International Telecommunication Union has scheduled a Cop31 event for November 16 on financing cleaner digital infrastructure, measuring emissions, and promoting durable, repairable and reusable electronics. The message is important: sustainability cannot stop at greener electricity. It also concerns what technology organisations purchase, how long they keep it, and who pays for its environmental effects. When a software decision becomes a hardware bill Consider a computer that still works but cannot support a newer operating system. Windows 10’s regular support ended in October 2025, although Microsoft offers extended security updates for eligible consumer devices through October 2027. The transition does not make every older computer obsolete. Yet software support and compatibility can influence whether organisations replace otherwise usable equipment. Manufacturing devices consumes energy and raw materials. It also creates electronic waste (e-waste). According to the UN’s global e-waste monitor, the world generated 62 million metric tonnes of e-waste in 2022, of which just 22.3% was documented as formally collected and recycled. These figures cover all electronic waste, not waste attributable to Microsoft. They nevertheless show why extending equipment lifetimes deserves a place in climate policy. What are the environmental costs of using data and digital? Costs that are rarely counted A software subscription has a visible price. Less visible are the costs of training employees, migrating files, replacing equipment, maintaining duplicate systems and eventually switching suppliers. Economists call these switching costs. They can lock organisations into existing providers even when better-value alternatives emerge. This is not merely hypothetical. In March 2026, the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority announced plans to investigate Microsoft’s business software ecosystem. It also reported steps by major cloud service providers, including Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services, to reduce data-transfer fees and improve interoperability, making it easier for businesses to switch between providers. What might this have to do with sustainability? A buyer unable to change providers easily may also struggle to choose lower-emission computing services. That is a potential environmental consequence of lock-in, not a demonstrated claim that Microsoft users emit more carbon. There is a wider accounting problem too. The UN estimates that global electronic waste was associated with approximately US$78 billion (£59 billion) in externalised costs in 2022, including pollution and climate-related impacts. Such costs are largely absent from the price of a software license. A responsible procurement decision should therefore compare lifetime financial costs, equipment lifespans and credible emissions data rather than only the next annual bill. Freedom to choose Could workplaces use alternatives (such as Thunderbird and LibreOffice) or interoperable cloud services? Often, yes. But migration has costs and a rival provider is not necessarily greener. The better goal is freedom to choose: portable data, open document formats, repairable devices, transparent environmental reporting and software contracts that do not penalise switching. Digital systems that remain affordable, competitive and environmentally responsible, even when their preferred technology changes, will be the most resilient ones. Narmin Nahidi does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
